Infinite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes

Finite-horizon stochastic dynamic programming obtains its boundary condition from the terminal reward. What value equation remains when the process has no terminal date? Discounting makes the infinite reward stream bounded and turns the Bellman equations into fixed-point problems.

The undiscounted expected total reward of policy π∈ΠHR\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{\mathrm{HR}}π∈ΠHR is

vπ(s)=E[∑t=1∞r(St,At)]v^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} r(S_t, A_t)\right]vπ(s)=E[t=1∑∞​r(St​,At​)]
(1)

One drawback of this model is that we could easily encounter values that are +∞+\infty+∞ or −∞-\infty−∞, even in a setting as simple as a single-state MDP which loops back into itself and where the accrued reward is nonzero.

Therefore, it is often more convenient to work with an alternative formulation which guarantees the existence of a limit: the expected total discounted reward of policy π∈ΠHR\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{\mathrm{HR}}π∈ΠHR is defined to be:

vγπ(s)≡lim⁡N→∞E[∑t=1Nγt−1r(St,At)]v_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) \equiv \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^N \gamma^{t-1} r(S_t, A_t)\right]vγπ​(s)≡N→∞lim​E[t=1∑N​γt−1r(St​,At​)]
(2)

for 0≤γ<10 \leq \gamma < 10≤γ<1 and when max⁡s∈Smax⁡a∈As∣r(s,a)∣=Rmax⁡<∞\max_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s}|r(s, a)| = R_{\max} < \inftymaxs∈S​maxa∈As​​∣r(s,a)∣=Rmax​<∞, in which case, ∣vγπ(s)∣≤(1−γ)−1Rmax⁡|v_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s)| \leq (1-\gamma)^{-1} R_{\max}∣vγπ​(s)∣≤(1−γ)−1Rmax​.

Finally, another possibility for the infinite-horizon setting is the so-called average reward or gain of policy π∈ΠHR\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{\mathrm{HR}}π∈ΠHR defined as:

gπ(s)≡lim⁡N→∞1NE[∑t=1Nr(St,At)]g^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) \equiv \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{N} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^N r(S_t, A_t)\right]gπ(s)≡N→∞lim​N1​E[t=1∑N​r(St​,At​)]
(3)

We won’t be working with this formulation in this course due to its inherent practical and theoretical complexities.

Extending the previous notion of optimality from finite-horizon models, a policy π∗\boldsymbol{\pi}^*π∗ is said to be discount optimal for a given γ\gammaγ if:

vγπ∗(s)≥vγπ(s) for each s∈S and all π∈ΠHRv_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}^*}(s) \geq v_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) \quad \text { for each } s \in S \text { and all } \boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{\mathrm{HR}}vγπ∗​(s)≥vγπ​(s) for each s∈S and all π∈ΠHR
(4)

Furthermore, the value of a discounted MDP, vγ∗(s)v_\gamma^*(s)vγ∗​(s), is defined by:

vγ∗(s)≡max⁡π∈ΠHRvγπ(s)v_\gamma^*(s) \equiv \max _{\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{\mathrm{HR}}} v_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s)vγ∗​(s)≡π∈ΠHRmax​vγπ​(s)
(5)

More often, we refer to vγv_\gammavγ​ by simply calling it the optimal value function.

As for the finite-horizon setting, the infinite horizon discounted model does not require history-dependent policies, since for any π∈ΠHR\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{HR}π∈ΠHR there exists a π′∈ΠMR\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime} \in \Pi^{MR}π′∈ΠMR with identical total discounted reward:

vγ∗(s)≡max⁡π∈ΠHRvγπ(s)=max⁡π∈ΠMRvγπ(s).v_\gamma^*(s) \equiv \max_{\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{HR}} v_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s)=\max_{\boldsymbol{\pi} \in \Pi^{MR}} v_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) .vγ∗​(s)≡π∈ΠHRmax​vγπ​(s)=π∈ΠMRmax​vγπ​(s).
(6)

Random Horizon Interpretation of Discounting¶

Can geometric termination give the discount factor a probabilistic meaning rather than treating it only as an algebraic device? The use of discounting can be motivated both from a modeling perspective and as a means to ensure that the total reward remains bounded. From the modeling perspective, we can view discounting as a way to put more or less weight on the immediate rewards vs. the long-term consequences. There is also another interpretation which stems from that of a finite horizon model but with an uncertain end time. More precisely:

Let vνπ(s)v_\nu^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s)vνπ​(s) denote the expected total reward obtained by using policy π\boldsymbol{\pi}π when the horizon length ν\nuν is random. We define it by:

vνπ(s)≡Esπ[Eν{∑t=1νr(St,At)}]v_\nu^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) \equiv \mathbb{E}_s^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\left[\mathbb{E}_\nu\left\{\sum_{t=1}^\nu r(S_t, A_t)\right\}\right]vνπ​(s)≡Esπ​[Eν​{t=1∑ν​r(St​,At​)}]
(7)
Theorem 1 (Random horizon interpretation of discounting)

Suppose that the horizon ν\nuν follows a geometric distribution with parameter γ\gammaγ, 0≤γ<10 \leq \gamma < 10≤γ<1, independent of the policy such that P(ν=n)=(1−γ)γn−1, n=1,2,…P(\nu=n) = (1-\gamma) \gamma^{n-1}, \, n=1,2, \ldotsP(ν=n)=(1−γ)γn−1,n=1,2,…, then vνπ(s)=vγπ(s)v_\nu^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) = v_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s)vνπ​(s)=vγπ​(s) for all s∈Ss \in \mathcal{S}s∈S .

Proof 1

See proposition 5.3.1 in Puterman (1994).

By definition of the finite-horizon value function and the law of total expectation:

vνπ(s)=∑n=1∞P(ν=n)⋅vnπ(s)=∑n=1∞(1−γ)γn−1⋅Esπ{∑t=1nr(St,At)}.v_\nu^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P(\nu=n) \cdot v_n^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (1-\gamma) \gamma^{n-1} \cdot E_s^{\boldsymbol{\pi}} \left\{\sum_{t=1}^n r(S_t, A_t)\right\}.vνπ​(s)=n=1∑∞​P(ν=n)⋅vnπ​(s)=n=1∑∞​(1−γ)γn−1⋅Esπ​{t=1∑n​r(St​,At​)}.
(8)

Combining the expectation with the sum over nnn:

vνπ(s)=Esπ{∑n=1∞(1−γ)γn−1∑t=1nr(St,At)}.v_\nu^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) = E_s^{\boldsymbol{\pi}} \left\{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (1-\gamma) \gamma^{n-1} \sum_{t=1}^n r(S_t, A_t)\right\}.vνπ​(s)=Esπ​{n=1∑∞​(1−γ)γn−1t=1∑n​r(St​,At​)}.
(9)

Reordering the summations: Under the bounded reward assumption ∣r(s,a)∣≤Rmax⁡|r(s,a)| \leq R_{\max}∣r(s,a)∣≤Rmax​ and γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1, we have

Esπ{∑n=1∞∑t=1n∣r(St,At)∣⋅(1−γ)γn−1}≤Rmax⁡∑n=1∞n(1−γ)γn−1=Rmax⁡1−γ<∞,E_s^{\boldsymbol{\pi}} \left\{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \sum_{t=1}^n |r(S_t, A_t)| \cdot (1-\gamma) \gamma^{n-1}\right\} \leq R_{\max} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n (1-\gamma) \gamma^{n-1} = \frac{R_{\max}}{1-\gamma} < \infty,Esπ​{n=1∑∞​t=1∑n​∣r(St​,At​)∣⋅(1−γ)γn−1}≤Rmax​n=1∑∞​n(1−γ)γn−1=1−γRmax​​<∞,
(10)

which justifies exchanging the order of summation by Fubini’s theorem.

To reverse the order, note that the pair (n,t)(n,t)(n,t) with 1≤t≤n1 \leq t \leq n1≤t≤n can be reindexed by fixing ttt first and letting nnn range from ttt to ∞\infty∞:

∑n=1∞∑t=1n=∑t=1∞∑n=t∞.\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \sum_{t=1}^n = \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \sum_{n=t}^{\infty}.n=1∑∞​t=1∑n​=t=1∑∞​n=t∑∞​.
(11)

Therefore:

vνπ(s)=Esπ{∑t=1∞r(St,At)∑n=t∞(1−γ)γn−1}.\begin{align*} v_\nu^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) &= E_s^{\boldsymbol{\pi}} \left\{\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} r(S_t, A_t) \sum_{n=t}^{\infty} (1-\gamma) \gamma^{n-1}\right\}. \end{align*}vνπ​(s)​=Esπ​{t=1∑∞​r(St​,At​)n=t∑∞​(1−γ)γn−1}.​
(12)

Evaluating the inner sum: Using the substitution m=n−t+1m = n - t + 1m=n−t+1 (so n=m+t−1n = m + t - 1n=m+t−1):

∑n=t∞(1−γ)γn−1=∑m=1∞(1−γ)γm+t−2=γt−1(1−γ)∑m=1∞γm−1=γt−1(1−γ)⋅11−γ=γt−1.\begin{align*} \sum_{n=t}^{\infty} (1-\gamma) \gamma^{n-1} &= \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} (1-\gamma) \gamma^{m+t-2} \\ &= \gamma^{t-1} (1-\gamma) \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \gamma^{m-1} \\ &= \gamma^{t-1} (1-\gamma) \cdot \frac{1}{1-\gamma} = \gamma^{t-1}. \end{align*}n=t∑∞​(1−γ)γn−1​=m=1∑∞​(1−γ)γm+t−2=γt−1(1−γ)m=1∑∞​γm−1=γt−1(1−γ)⋅1−γ1​=γt−1.​
(13)

Substituting back:

vνπ(s)=Esπ{∑t=1∞γt−1r(St,At)}=vγπ(s).v_\nu^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) = E_s^{\boldsymbol{\pi}} \left\{\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \gamma^{t-1} r(S_t, A_t)\right\} = v_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s).vνπ​(s)=Esπ​{t=1∑∞​γt−1r(St​,At​)}=vγπ​(s).
(14)

Vector Representation in Markov Decision Processes¶

How do transition kernels, rewards, and policies become matrices and vectors that expose the Bellman equations as operator equations?

Let V be the set of bounded real-valued functions on a discrete state space S. This means any function f∈V f \in V f∈V satisfies the condition:

∥f∥=max⁡s∈S∣f(s)∣<∞.\|f\| = \max_{s \in S} |f(s)| < \infty.∥f∥=s∈Smax​∣f(s)∣<∞.
(15)

where the notation ∥f∥ \|f\| ∥f∥ represents the sup-norm (or ℓ∞ \ell_\infty ℓ∞​-norm) of the function f f f.

When working with discrete state spaces, we can interpret elements of V as vectors and linear operators on V as matrices, allowing us to leverage tools from linear algebra. The sup-norm (ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ norm) of matrix H\mathbf{H}H is defined as:

∥H∥≡max⁡s∈S∑j∈S∣Hs,j∣\|\mathbf{H}\| \equiv \max_{s \in S} \sum_{j \in S} |\mathbf{H}_{s,j}|∥H∥≡s∈Smax​j∈S∑​∣Hs,j​∣
(16)

where Hs,j\mathbf{H}_{s,j}Hs,j​ represents the (s,j)(s, j)(s,j)-th component of the matrix H\mathbf{H}H.

For a Markovian decision rule π∈ΠMD\pi \in \Pi^{MD}π∈ΠMD, we define:

rπ(s)≡r(s,π(s)),rπ∈R∣S∣,[Pπ]s,j≡p(j∣s,π(s)),Pπ∈R∣S∣×∣S∣.\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}_\pi(s) &\equiv r(s, \pi(s)), \quad \mathbf{r}_\pi \in \mathbb{R}^{|S|}, \\ [\mathbf{P}_\pi]_{s,j} &\equiv p(j \mid s, \pi(s)), \quad \mathbf{P}_\pi \in \mathbb{R}^{|S| \times |S|}. \end{align*}rπ​(s)[Pπ​]s,j​​≡r(s,π(s)),rπ​∈R∣S∣,≡p(j∣s,π(s)),Pπ​∈R∣S∣×∣S∣.​
(17)

For a randomized decision rule π∈ΠMR\pi \in \Pi^{MR}π∈ΠMR, these definitions extend to:

rπ(s)≡∑a∈Asπ(a∣s) r(s,a),[Pπ]s,j≡∑a∈Asπ(a∣s) p(j∣s,a).\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}_\pi(s) &\equiv \sum_{a \in A_s} \pi(a \mid s) \, r(s, a), \\ [\mathbf{P}_\pi]_{s,j} &\equiv \sum_{a \in A_s} \pi(a \mid s) \, p(j \mid s, a). \end{align*}rπ​(s)[Pπ​]s,j​​≡a∈As​∑​π(a∣s)r(s,a),≡a∈As​∑​π(a∣s)p(j∣s,a).​
(18)

In both cases, rπ\mathbf{r}_\pirπ​ denotes a reward vector in R∣S∣\mathbb{R}^{|S|}R∣S∣, with each component rπ(s)\mathbf{r}_\pi(s)rπ​(s) representing the reward associated with state sss. Similarly, Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​ is a transition probability matrix in R∣S∣×∣S∣\mathbb{R}^{|S| \times |S|}R∣S∣×∣S∣, capturing the transition probabilities under decision rule π\piπ.

For a nonstationary Markovian policy π=(π1,π2,…)∈ΠMR\boldsymbol{\pi} = (\pi_1, \pi_2, \ldots) \in \Pi^{MR}π=(π1​,π2​,…)∈ΠMR, the expected total discounted reward is given by:

vγπ(s)=E[∑t=1∞γt−1r(St,At) | S1=s].\mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s)=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \gamma^{t-1} r\left(S_t, A_t\right) \,\middle|\, S_1 = s\right].vγπ​(s)=E[t=1∑∞​γt−1r(St​,At​)∣∣​S1​=s].
(19)

Using vector notation, this can be expressed as:

vγπ=∑t=1∞γt−1Pπt−1rπ1=rπ1+γPπ1rπ2+γ2Pπ1Pπ2rπ3+⋯=rπ1+γPπ1(rπ2+γPπ2rπ3+γ2Pπ2Pπ3rπ4+⋯ ).\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}} &= \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \gamma^{t-1} \mathbf{P}_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{t-1} \mathbf{r}_{\pi_1} \\ &= \mathbf{r}_{\pi_1} + \gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_1} \mathbf{r}_{\pi_2} + \gamma^2 \mathbf{P}_{\pi_1} \mathbf{P}_{\pi_2} \mathbf{r}_{\pi_3} + \cdots \\ &= \mathbf{r}_{\pi_1} + \gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_1} \left( \mathbf{r}_{\pi_2} + \gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_2} \mathbf{r}_{\pi_3} + \gamma^2 \mathbf{P}_{\pi_2} \mathbf{P}_{\pi_3} \mathbf{r}_{\pi_4} + \cdots \right). \end{aligned}vγπ​​=t=1∑∞​γt−1Pπt−1​rπ1​​=rπ1​​+γPπ1​​rπ2​​+γ2Pπ1​​Pπ2​​rπ3​​+⋯=rπ1​​+γPπ1​​(rπ2​​+γPπ2​​rπ3​​+γ2Pπ2​​Pπ3​​rπ4​​+⋯).​
(20)

This formulation leads to a recursive relationship:

vγπ=rπ1+γPπ1vγπ′=∑t=1∞γt−1Pπt−1rπt\begin{align*} \mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}} &= \mathbf{r}_{\pi_1} + \gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_1} \mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}}\\ &=\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \gamma^{t-1} \mathbf{P}_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{t-1} \mathbf{r}_{\pi_t} \end{align*}vγπ​​=rπ1​​+γPπ1​​vγπ′​=t=1∑∞​γt−1Pπt−1​rπt​​​
(21)

where π′=(π2,π3,…)\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime} = (\pi_2, \pi_3, \ldots)π′=(π2​,π3​,…).

For a stationary policy π=const(π)\boldsymbol{\pi} = \mathrm{const}(\pi)π=const(π) with constant decision rule π\piπ, the total expected reward simplifies to:

vγπ=rπ+γPπvγπ=∑t=1∞γt−1Pπt−1rπ\begin{align*} \mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\pi} &= \mathbf{r}_\pi+ \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\pi} \\ &=\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \gamma^{t-1} \mathbf{P}_\pi^{t-1} \mathbf{r}_{\pi} \end{align*}vγπ​​=rπ​+γPπ​vγπ​=t=1∑∞​γt−1Pπt−1​rπ​​
(22)

This last expression is called a Neumann series expansion, and it’s guaranteed to exist under the assumptions of bounded reward and discount factor strictly less than one.

Theorem 2 (Neumann Series and Invertibility)

The spectral radius of a matrix H\mathbf{H}H is defined as:

ρ(H)≡max⁡i∣λi(H)∣\rho(\mathbf{H}) \equiv \max_{i} |\lambda_i(\mathbf{H})|ρ(H)≡imax​∣λi​(H)∣
(23)

where λi(H)\lambda_i(\mathbf{H})λi​(H) are the eigenvalues of H\mathbf{H}H.

Neumann Series Existence: For any matrix H\mathbf{H}H, the Neumann series

∑t=0∞Ht=I+H+H2+⋯\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \mathbf{H}^t = \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{H} + \mathbf{H}^2 + \cdotst=0∑∞​Ht=I+H+H2+⋯
(24)

converges if and only if ρ(H)<1\rho(\mathbf{H}) < 1ρ(H)<1. When this condition holds, the matrix (I−H)(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})(I−H) is invertible and

(I−H)−1=∑t=0∞Ht.(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H})^{-1} = \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \mathbf{H}^t.(I−H)−1=t=0∑∞​Ht.
(25)

Note that for any induced matrix norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|∥⋅∥ (i.e., a norm satisfying ∥Hv∥≤∥H∥⋅∥v∥\|\mathbf{H}\mathbf{v}\| \leq \|\mathbf{H}\| \cdot \|\mathbf{v}\|∥Hv∥≤∥H∥⋅∥v∥ for all vectors v\mathbf{v}v) and any matrix H\mathbf{H}H, the spectral radius is bounded by:

ρ(H)≤∥H∥.\rho(\mathbf{H}) \leq \|\mathbf{H}\|.ρ(H)≤∥H∥.
(26)

This inequality provides a practical way to verify the convergence condition ρ(H)<1\rho(\mathbf{H}) < 1ρ(H)<1 by checking the simpler condition ∥H∥<1\|\mathbf{H}\| < 1∥H∥<1 rather than trying to compute the eigenvalues directly.

We can now verify that (I−γPπ)(\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi)(I−γPπ​) is invertible and the Neumann series converges.

  1. Norm of the transition matrix: Since Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​ is a stochastic matrix (each row sums to 1 and all entries are non-negative), its ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​-norm is:

    ∥Pπ∥=max⁡s∈S∑j∈S[Pπ]s,j=max⁡s∈S1=1.\|\mathbf{P}_\pi\| = \max_{s \in S} \sum_{j \in S} [\mathbf{P}_\pi]_{s,j} = \max_{s \in S} 1 = 1.∥Pπ​∥=s∈Smax​j∈S∑​[Pπ​]s,j​=s∈Smax​1=1.
    (27)

  2. Norm of the scaled matrix: Using the homogeneity property of norms, we have:

    ∥γPπ∥=∣γ∣⋅∥Pπ∥=∣γ∣⋅1=∣γ∣.\|\gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi\| = |\gamma| \cdot \|\mathbf{P}_\pi\| = |\gamma| \cdot 1 = |\gamma|.∥γPπ​∥=∣γ∣⋅∥Pπ​∥=∣γ∣⋅1=∣γ∣.
    (28)

  3. Bounding the spectral radius: Since the spectral radius is bounded by the matrix norm:

    ρ(γPπ)≤∥γPπ∥=∣γ∣.\rho(\gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi) \leq \|\gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi\| = |\gamma|.ρ(γPπ​)≤∥γPπ​∥=∣γ∣.
    (29)

  4. Verifying convergence: Since 0≤γ<10 \leq \gamma < 10≤γ<1 by assumption, we have:

    ρ(γPπ)≤∣γ∣<1.\rho(\gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi) \leq |\gamma| < 1.ρ(γPπ​)≤∣γ∣<1.
    (30)

    This strict inequality guarantees that (I−γPπ)(\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi)(I−γPπ​) is invertible and the Neumann series converges.

Therefore, the Neumann series expansion converges and yields:

vγπ=(I−γPπ)−1rπ=∑t=0∞(γPπ)trπ=∑t=1∞γt−1Pπt−1rπ.\mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\pi} = (\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi)^{-1} \mathbf{r}_\pi = \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} (\gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi)^t \mathbf{r}_\pi = \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \gamma^{t-1} \mathbf{P}_\pi^{t-1} \mathbf{r}_\pi.vγπ​=(I−γPπ​)−1rπ​=t=0∑∞​(γPπ​)trπ​=t=1∑∞​γt−1Pπt−1​rπ​.
(31)

Consequently, for a stationary policy, vγπ\mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\pi}vγπ​ can be determined as the solution to the linear equation:

v=rπ+γPπv,\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{r}_\pi+ \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{v},v=rπ​+γPπ​v,
(32)

which can be rearranged to:

(I−γPπ)v=rπ.(\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi) \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{r}_\pi.(I−γPπ​)v=rπ​.
(33)

We can also characterize vγπ\mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\pi}vγπ​ as the solution to an operator equation. More specifically, define the transformation Lπ\mathrm{L}_\piLπ​ by

Lπv≡rπ+γPπv\mathrm{L}_\pi \mathbf{v} \equiv \mathbf{r}_\pi+\gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{v}Lπ​v≡rπ​+γPπ​v
(34)

for any v∈V\mathbf{v} \in Vv∈V. Intuitively, Lπ\mathrm{L}_\piLπ​ takes a value function v\mathbf{v}v as input and returns a new value function that combines immediate rewards (rπ\mathbf{r}_\pirπ​) with discounted future values (γPπv\gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{v}γPπ​v).

Note

While we often refer to Lπ\mathrm{L}_\piLπ​ as a “linear operator” in the RL literature, it is technically an affine operator (or affine transformation), not a linear operator in the strict sense. To see why, recall that a linear operator T\mathcal{T}T must satisfy:

  1. Additivity: T(v1+v2)=T(v1)+T(v2)\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2) = \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{v}_1) + \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{v}_2)T(v1​+v2​)=T(v1​)+T(v2​)

  2. Homogeneity: T(αv)=αT(v)\mathcal{T}(\alpha \mathbf{v}) = \alpha \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{v})T(αv)=αT(v) for all scalars α\alphaα

However, Lπ\mathrm{L}_\piLπ​ fails the additivity test:

Lπ(v1+v2)=rπ+γPπ(v1+v2)=rπ+γPπv1+γPπv2\mathrm{L}_\pi(\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2) = \mathbf{r}_\pi + \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi(\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2) = \mathbf{r}_\pi + \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{v}_1 + \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{v}_2Lπ​(v1​+v2​)=rπ​+γPπ​(v1​+v2​)=rπ​+γPπ​v1​+γPπ​v2​
(35)

while

Lπ(v1)+Lπ(v2)=(rπ+γPπv1)+(rπ+γPπv2)=2rπ+γPπv1+γPπv2.\mathrm{L}_\pi(\mathbf{v}_1) + \mathrm{L}_\pi(\mathbf{v}_2) = (\mathbf{r}_\pi + \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{v}_1) + (\mathbf{r}_\pi + \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{v}_2) = 2\mathbf{r}_\pi + \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{v}_1 + \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{v}_2.Lπ​(v1​)+Lπ​(v2​)=(rπ​+γPπ​v1​)+(rπ​+γPπ​v2​)=2rπ​+γPπ​v1​+γPπ​v2​.
(36)

The presence of the constant term rπ\mathbf{r}_\pirπ​ makes Lπ\mathrm{L}_\piLπ​ affine rather than linear. An affine operator has the form A(v)=b+T(v)\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{b} + \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{v})A(v)=b+T(v), where b\mathbf{b}b is a constant vector and T\mathcal{T}T is a linear operator. In our case, b=rπ\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{r}_\pib=rπ​ and T(v)=γPπv\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{v}) = \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi\mathbf{v}T(v)=γPπ​v.

Despite this technical distinction, the term “linear operator” is commonly used in the reinforcement learning literature when referring to Lπ\mathrm{L}_\piLπ​, following a slight abuse of terminology.

Therefore, we view Lπ\mathrm{L}_\piLπ​ as an operator mapping elements of VVV to VVV: i.e., Lπ:V→V\mathrm{L}_\pi: V \rightarrow VLπ​:V→V. The fact that the value function of a policy is the solution to a fixed-point equation can then be expressed with the statement:

vγπ=Lπvγπ.\mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\pi}=\mathrm{L}_\pi \mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\pi}.vγπ​=Lπ​vγπ​.
(37)

This is a fixed-point equation: the value function vγπ\mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\pi}vγπ​ is a fixed point of the operator Lπ\mathrm{L}_\piLπ​.

Solving Operator Equations¶

Which iterative and Newton-like methods solve a fixed point when direct matrix inversion is unavailable or inappropriate?

The operator equation we encountered in MDPs, vγπ=Lπvγπ\mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\pi} = \mathrm{L}_\pi \mathbf{v}_\gamma^{\pi}vγπ​=Lπ​vγπ​, is a specific instance of a more general class of problems known as operator equations. These equations appear in various fields of mathematics and applied sciences, ranging from differential equations to functional analysis.

Operator equations can take several forms, each with its own characteristics and solution methods:

  1. Fixed Point Form: x=T(x)x = \mathrm{T}(x)x=T(x), where T:X→X\mathrm{T}: X \rightarrow XT:X→X. This form is common in fixed-point problems, such as our MDP equation: we seek a fixed point x∗x^*x∗ such that x∗=T(x∗)x^* = \mathrm{T}(x^*)x∗=T(x∗).

  2. General Operator Equation: T(x)=y\mathrm{T}(x) = yT(x)=y, where T:X→Y\mathrm{T}: X \rightarrow YT:X→Y. Here, XXX and YYY can be different spaces. We seek an x∈Xx \in Xx∈X that satisfies the equation for a given y∈Yy \in Yy∈Y.

  3. Nonlinear Equation: T(x)=0\mathrm{T}(x) = 0T(x)=0, where T:X→Y\mathrm{T}: X \rightarrow YT:X→Y. A special case of the general operator equation where we seek roots or zeros of the operator.

  4. Variational Inequality: Find x∗∈Kx^* \in Kx∗∈K such that ⟨T(x∗),x−x∗⟩≥0\langle \mathrm{T}(x^*), x - x^* \rangle \geq 0⟨T(x∗),x−x∗⟩≥0 for all x∈Kx \in Kx∈K. Here, KKK is a closed convex subset of XXX, and T:K→X∗\mathrm{T}: K \rightarrow X^*T:K→X∗ (the dual space of XXX). These problems often arise in optimization, game theory, and partial differential equations.

Successive Approximation Method¶

For equations in fixed point form, a common numerical solution method is successive approximation, also known as fixed-point iteration:

Algorithm 1 (Successive Approximation)

Input: An operator T:X→X\mathrm{T}: X \rightarrow XT:X→X, an initial guess x0∈Xx_0 \in Xx0​∈X, and a tolerance ϵ>0\epsilon > 0ϵ>0
Output: An approximate fixed point x∗x^*x∗ such that ∥x∗−T(x∗)∥<ϵ\|x^* - \mathrm{T}(x^*)\| < \epsilon∥x∗−T(x∗)∥<ϵ

  1. Initialize n=0n = 0n=0

  2. repeat
    3. Compute xn+1=T(xn)x_{n+1} = \mathrm{T}(x_n)xn+1​=T(xn​)
    4. If ∥xn+1−xn∥<ϵ\|x_{n+1} - x_n\| < \epsilon∥xn+1​−xn​∥<ϵ, return xn+1x_{n+1}xn+1​
    5. Set n=n+1n = n + 1n=n+1

  3. until convergence or maximum iterations reached

The convergence of successive approximation depends on the properties of the operator T\mathrm{T}T. In the simplest and most common setting, we assume T\mathrm{T}T is a contraction mapping. The Banach Fixed-Point Theorem then guarantees that T\mathrm{T}T has a unique fixed point, and the successive approximation method will converge to this fixed point from any starting point. Specifically, T\mathrm{T}T is a contraction if there exists a constant q∈[0,1)q \in [0,1)q∈[0,1) such that for all x,y∈Xx,y \in Xx,y∈X:

d(T(x),T(y))≤q⋅d(x,y)d(\mathrm{T}(x), \mathrm{T}(y)) \leq q \cdot d(x,y)d(T(x),T(y))≤q⋅d(x,y)
(38)

where ddd is the metric on XXX. In this case, the rate of convergence is linear, with error bound:

d(xn,x∗)≤qn1−qd(x1,x0)d(x_n, x^*) \leq \frac{q^n}{1-q} d(x_1, x_0)d(xn​,x∗)≤1−qqn​d(x1​,x0​)
(39)

However, the contraction mapping condition is not the only one that can lead to convergence. For instance, if T\mathrm{T}T is nonexpansive (i.e., Lipschitz continuous with Lipschitz constant 1) and XXX is a Banach space with certain geometrical properties (e.g., uniformly convex), then under additional conditions (e.g., T\mathrm{T}T has at least one fixed point), the successive approximation method can still converge, albeit potentially more slowly than in the contraction case.

In practice, when dealing with specific problems like MDPs or differential equations, the properties of the operator often naturally align with one of these convergence conditions. For example, in discounted MDPs, the Bellman operator is a contraction in the supremum norm, which guarantees the convergence of value iteration.

Newton-Kantorovich Method¶

The Newton-Kantorovich method is a generalization of Newton’s method from finite dimensional vector spaces to infinite dimensional function spaces: rather than iterating in the space of vectors, we are iterating in the space of functions.

Newton’s method is often written as the familiar update:

xk+1=xk−[DF(xk)]−1F(xk),x_{k+1} = x_k - [DF(x_k)]^{-1} F(x_k),xk+1​=xk​−[DF(xk​)]−1F(xk​),
(40)

which makes it look as though the essence of the method is “take a derivative and invert it.” But the real workhorse behind Newton’s method (both in finite and infinite dimensions) is linearization.

At each step, the idea is to replace the nonlinear operator F:X→YF:X \to YF:X→Y by a local surrogate model of the form

F(x+h)≈F(x)+Lh,F(x+h) \approx F(x) + Lh,F(x+h)≈F(x)+Lh,
(41)

where LLL is a linear map capturing how small perturbations in the input propagate to changes in the output. This is a Taylor-like expansion in Banach spaces: the role of the derivative is precisely to provide the correct notion of such a linear operator.

To find a root of FFF, we impose the condition that the surrogate vanishes at the next iterate:

0=F(x+h)≈F(x)+Lh.0 = F(x+h) \approx F(x) + Lh.0=F(x+h)≈F(x)+Lh.
(42)

Solving this linear equation gives the increment hhh. In finite dimensions, LLL is the Jacobian matrix; in Banach spaces, it must be the Fréchet derivative.

But what exactly is a Fréchet derivative in infinite dimensions? To understand this, we need to generalize the concept of derivative from finite-dimensional calculus. In infinite-dimensional spaces, there are several notions of differentiability, each with different strengths and requirements:

1. Gâteaux (Directional) Derivative

We say that the Gâteaux derivative of FFF at xxx in a specific direction hhh is:

F′(x;h)=lim⁡t→0F(x+th)−F(x)tF'(x; h) = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{F(x + th) - F(x)}{t}F′(x;h)=t→0lim​tF(x+th)−F(x)​
(43)

This quantity measures how the function FFF changes along the ray x+thx + thx+th. While this limit may exist for each direction hhh separately, it doesn’t guarantee that the derivative is linear in hhh. This is a key limitation: the Gâteaux derivative can exist in all directions but still fail to provide a good linear approximation.

2. Hadamard Directional Derivative

Rather than considering a single direction of perturbation, we now consider a bundle of perturbations around hhh. We ask how the function changes as we approach the target direction from nearby directions. We say that FFF has a Hadamard directional derivative if:

F′(x;h)=lim⁡t↓0h′→hF(x+th′)−F(x)tF'(x; h) = \lim_{\substack{t \downarrow 0 \\ h' \to h}} \frac{F(x + t h') - F(x)}{t}F′(x;h)=t↓0h′→h​lim​tF(x+th′)−F(x)​
(44)

This is a stronger condition than Gâteaux differentiability because it requires the limit to be uniform over nearby directions. However, it still doesn’t guarantee linearity in hhh.

3. Fréchet Derivative

The strongest and most natural notion: FFF is Fréchet differentiable at xxx if there exists a bounded linear operator LLL such that:

lim⁡h→0∥F(x+h)−F(x)−Lh∥∥h∥=0\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\|F(x + h) - F(x) - Lh\|}{\|h\|} = 0h→0lim​∥h∥∥F(x+h)−F(x)−Lh∥​=0
(45)

This definition directly addresses the inadequacy of the previous notions. Unlike Gâteaux and Hadamard derivatives, the Fréchet derivative explicitly requires the existence of a linear operator LLL that provides a good approximation. Key properties:

  • LLL must be linear in hhh (unlike the directional derivatives above)

  • The approximation error is o(∥h∥)o(\|h\|)o(∥h∥), uniform in all directions

  • This is the “true” derivative: it generalizes the Jacobian matrix to infinite dimensions

  • Notation: L=F′(x)L = F'(x)L=F′(x) or DF(x)DF(x)DF(x)

Relationship:

Freˊchet differentiable⇒Hadamard directionally diff.⇒Gaˆteaux directionally diff.\text{Fréchet differentiable} \Rightarrow \text{Hadamard directionally diff.} \Rightarrow \text{Gâteaux directionally diff.}Freˊchet differentiable⇒Hadamard directionally diff.⇒Gaˆteaux directionally diff.
(46)

In the context of the Newton-Kantorovich method, we work with an operator F:X→YF: X \to YF:X→Y where both XXX and YYY are Banach spaces. The Fréchet derivative F′(x)F'(x)F′(x) is the best linear approximation of FFF near xxx, and it’s exactly this linear operator LLL that we use in our linearization F(x+h)≈F(x)+F′(x)hF(x+h) \approx F(x) + F'(x)hF(x+h)≈F(x)+F′(x)h.

Now apart from those mathematical technicalities, Newton-Kantorovich has in essence the same structure as that of the original Newton’s method. That is, it applies the following sequence of steps:

  1. Linearize the Operator: Given an approximation xn x_n xn​, we consider the Fréchet derivative of F F F, denoted by F′(xn) F'(x_n) F′(xn​). This derivative is a linear operator that provides a local approximation of F F F near xn x_n xn​.

  2. Set Up the Newton Step: The method then solves the linearized equation for a correction hn h_n hn​:

    F′(xn)hn=−F(xn).F'(x_n) h_n = -F(x_n).F′(xn​)hn​=−F(xn​).
    (47)

    This equation represents a linear system where hn h_n hn​ is chosen so that the linearized operator F(xn)+F′(xn)hn F(x_n) + F'(x_n)h_n F(xn​)+F′(xn​)hn​ equals zero.

  3. Update the Solution: The new approximation xn+1 x_{n+1} xn+1​ is then given by:

    xn+1=xn+hn.x_{n+1} = x_n + h_n.xn+1​=xn​+hn​.
    (48)

    This correction step refines xn x_n xn​, bringing it closer to the true solution.

  4. Repeat Until Convergence: We repeat the linearization and update steps until the solution xn x_n xn​ converges to the desired tolerance, which can be verified by checking that ∥F(xn)∥ \|F(x_n)\| ∥F(xn​)∥ is sufficiently small, or by monitoring the norm ∥xn+1−xn∥ \|x_{n+1} - x_n\| ∥xn+1​−xn​∥.

The convergence of Newton-Kantorovich does not hinge on F F F being a contraction over the entire domain (as it could be the case for successive approximation). The convergence properties of the Newton-Kantorovich method are as follows:

  1. Local Convergence: Under mild conditions (e.g., FFF is Fréchet differentiable and F′(x)F'(x)F′(x) is invertible near the solution), the method converges locally. This means that if the initial guess is sufficiently close to the true solution, the method will converge.

  2. Global Convergence: Global convergence is not guaranteed in general. However, under stronger conditions (e.g., FFF is analytic and satisfies certain bounds), the method can converge globally.

  3. Rate of Convergence: When the method converges, it typically exhibits quadratic convergence. This means that the error at each step is proportional to the square of the error at the previous step:

    ∥xn+1−x∗∥≤C∥xn−x∗∥2\|x_{n+1} - x^*\| \leq C\|x_n - x^*\|^2∥xn+1​−x∗∥≤C∥xn​−x∗∥2
    (49)

    where x∗x^*x∗ is the true solution and CCC is some constant. This quadratic convergence is significantly faster than the linear convergence typically seen in methods like successive approximation.

Optimality Equations for Infinite-Horizon MDPs¶

How does actionwise maximization turn fixed-policy evaluation into the Bellman optimality equation?

Recall that in the finite-horizon setting, the optimality equations are:

vn(s)=max⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)vn+1(j)}v_n(s) = \max_{a \in A_s} \left\{r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in S} p(j | s, a) v_{n+1}(j)\right\}vn​(s)=a∈As​max​⎩⎨⎧​r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)vn+1​(j)⎭⎬⎫​
(50)

where vn(s)v_n(s)vn​(s) is the value function at time step nnn for state sss, AsA_sAs​ is the set of actions available in state sss, r(s,a)r(s, a)r(s,a) is the reward function, γ\gammaγ is the discount factor, and p(j∣s,a)p(j | s, a)p(j∣s,a) is the transition probability from state sss to state jjj given action aaa.

Intuitively, we would expect that by taking the limit of nnn to infinity, we might get the nonlinear equations:

v(s)=max⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)}v(s) = \max_{a \in A_s} \left\{r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in S} p(j | s, a) v(j)\right\}v(s)=a∈As​max​⎩⎨⎧​r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j)⎭⎬⎫​
(51)

which are called the optimality equations or Bellman equations for infinite-horizon MDPs.

We can adopt an operator-theoretic perspective by defining operators on the space VVV of bounded real-valued functions on the state space SSS. For a deterministic Markov rule π∈ΠMD\pi \in \Pi^{MD}π∈ΠMD, define the policy-evaluation operator:

(Lπv)(s)=r(s,π(s))+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,π(s))v(j)(\BellmanPi v)(s) = r(s,\pi(s)) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,\pi(s)) v(j)(Lπ​v)(s)=r(s,π(s))+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,π(s))v(j)
(52)

The Bellman optimality operator is then:

Lv≡max⁡π∈ΠMD{rπ+γPπv}\Bellman \mathbf{v} \equiv \max_{\pi \in \Pi^{MD}} \left\{\mathbf{r}_\pi + \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{v}\right\}Lv≡π∈ΠMDmax​{rπ​+γPπ​v}
(53)

where ΠMD\Pi^{MD}ΠMD is the set of Markov deterministic decision rules, rπ\mathbf{r}_\pirπ​ is the reward vector under decision rule π\piπ, and Pπ\mathbf{P}_\piPπ​ is the transition probability matrix under decision rule π\piπ.

Note that while we write max⁡π∈ΠMD\max_{\pi \in \Pi^{MD}}maxπ∈ΠMD​, we do not implement the above operator by enumerating all decision rules. Rather, the fact that we compare policies based on their value functions in a componentwise fashion means that maximizing over the space of Markovian deterministic rules reduces to the following update in component form:

(Lv)(s)=max⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)}(\Bellman \mathbf{v})(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j)\right\}(Lv)(s)=a∈As​max​⎩⎨⎧​r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j)⎭⎬⎫​
(54)

For convenience, we define the greedy selector Greedy(v)∈ΠMD\mathrm{Greedy}(v) \in \Pi^{MD}Greedy(v)∈ΠMD that extracts an optimal decision rule from a value function:

Greedy(v)(s)∈arg⁡max⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)}\mathrm{Greedy}(v)(s) \in \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j)\right\}Greedy(v)(s)∈arga∈As​max​⎩⎨⎧​r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j)⎭⎬⎫​
(55)

In Puterman’s terminology, such a greedy selector is called vvv-improving (or conserving when it achieves the maximum). This operator will be useful for expressing algorithms succinctly:

  • Value iteration: vk+1=Lvkv_{k+1} = \Bellman v_kvk+1​=Lvk​, then extract π=Greedy(v∗)\pi = \mathrm{Greedy}(v^*)π=Greedy(v∗)

  • Policy iteration: πk+1=Greedy(vπk)\pi_{k+1} = \mathrm{Greedy}(v^{\pi_k})πk+1​=Greedy(vπk​) with vπkv^{\pi_k}vπk​ solving v=Lπkvv = \mathrm{L}_{\pi_k}vv=Lπk​​v

The equivalence between these two forms can be shown mathematically, as demonstrated in the following proposition and proof.

Proposition 1

The operator L\BellmanL defined as a maximization over Markov deterministic decision rules:

(Lv)(s)=max⁡π∈ΠMD{r(s,π(s))+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,π(s))v(j)}(\Bellman \mathbf{v})(s) = \max_{\pi \in \Pi^{MD}} \left\{r(s,\pi(s)) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,\pi(s)) v(j)\right\}(Lv)(s)=π∈ΠMDmax​⎩⎨⎧​r(s,π(s))+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,π(s))v(j)⎭⎬⎫​
(56)

is equivalent to the componentwise maximization over actions:

(Lv)(s)=max⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)}(\Bellman \mathbf{v})(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j)\right\}(Lv)(s)=a∈As​max​⎩⎨⎧​r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j)⎭⎬⎫​
(57)
Proof 2

Fix sss. Let

Qv(s,a)≜r(s,a)+γ∑jp(j∣s,a) v(j).Q_v(s,a) \triangleq r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{j}p(j\mid s,a)\,v(j).Qv​(s,a)≜r(s,a)+γj∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j).
(58)

For any rule π∈ΠMD\pi \in \Pi^{MD}π∈ΠMD, we have (Lπv)(s)=Qv(s,π(s))≤max⁡a∈AsQv(s,a)(\BellmanPi v)(s)=Q_v(s,\pi(s))\le \max_{a\in\mathcal{A}_s}Q_v(s,a)(Lπ​v)(s)=Qv​(s,π(s))≤maxa∈As​​Qv​(s,a).

Taking the maximum over π\piπ gives

max⁡π∈ΠMD(Lπv)(s)≤max⁡a∈AsQv(s,a).\max_{\pi\in\Pi^{MD}}(\BellmanPi v)(s) \le \max_{a\in\mathcal{A}_s}Q_v(s,a).π∈ΠMDmax​(Lπ​v)(s)≤a∈As​max​Qv​(s,a).
(59)

Conversely, choose a greedy selector πv∈ΠMD\pi^v\in\Pi^{MD}πv∈ΠMD such that for each sss,

πv(s)∈arg⁡max⁡a∈AsQv(s,a)\pi^v(s)\in\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}_s}Q_v(s,a)πv(s)∈arga∈As​max​Qv​(s,a)
(60)

(possible since As\mathcal{A}_sAs​ is finite; otherwise use a measurable ε\varepsilonε-greedy selector). Then

(Lπvv)(s)=Qv(s,πv(s))=max⁡a∈AsQv(s,a),(\Bellman _{\pi^v}v)(s)=Q_v(s,\pi^v(s))=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}_s}Q_v(s,a),(Lπv​v)(s)=Qv​(s,πv(s))=a∈As​max​Qv​(s,a),
(61)

so max⁡π(Lπv)(s)≥max⁡aQv(s,a)\max_{\pi}(\BellmanPi v)(s)\ge \max_{a}Q_v(s,a)maxπ​(Lπ​v)(s)≥maxa​Qv​(s,a). Combining both inequalities yields equality.

Algorithms for Solving the Optimality Equations¶

What computational trade-off separates value iteration, policy evaluation, and policy improvement?

The optimality equations are operator equations. Therefore, we can apply general numerical methods to solve them. Applying the successive approximation method to the Bellman optimality equation yields a method known as “value iteration” in dynamic programming. A direct application of the blueprint for successive approximation yields the following algorithm:

Algorithm 2 (Value Iteration)

Input Given an MDP (S,A,P,R,γ)(S, A, P, R, \gamma)(S,A,P,R,γ) and tolerance ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0

Output Compute an ε\varepsilonε-optimal value function vvv and policy π\piπ

  1. Initialize v0(s)=0v_0(s) = 0v0​(s)=0 for all s∈Ss \in Ss∈S

  2. n←0n \leftarrow 0n←0

  3. repeat

    1. For each s∈Ss \in Ss∈S:

      1. vn+1(s)←(Lvn)(s)=max⁡a∈A{r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)vn(j)}v_{n+1}(s) \leftarrow (\Bellman v_n)(s) = \max_{a \in A} \left\{r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a)v_n(j)\right\}vn+1​(s)←(Lvn​)(s)=maxa∈A​{r(s,a)+γ∑j∈S​p(j∣s,a)vn​(j)}

    2. δ←∥vn+1−vn∥∞\delta \leftarrow \|v_{n+1} - v_n\|_\inftyδ←∥vn+1​−vn​∥∞​

    3. n←n+1n \leftarrow n + 1n←n+1

  4. until δ<ε(1−γ)2γ\delta < \frac{\varepsilon(1-\gamma)}{2\gamma}δ<2γε(1−γ)​

  5. Extract greedy policy: π←Greedy(vn)\pi \leftarrow \mathrm{Greedy}(v_n)π←Greedy(vn​) where

    Greedy(v)(s)∈arg⁡max⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)}\mathrm{Greedy}(v)(s) \in \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a)v(j)\right\}Greedy(v)(s)∈arga∈As​max​⎩⎨⎧​r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j)⎭⎬⎫​
    (62)

  6. return vn,πv_n, \pivn​,π

The termination criterion in this algorithm is based on a specific bound that provides guarantees on the quality of the solution. This is in contrast to supervised learning, where we often use arbitrary termination criteria based on computational budget or early stopping when the learning curve flattens. This is because establishing implementable generalization bounds in supervised learning is challenging.

However, in the dynamic programming context, we can derive various bounds that can be implemented in practice. These bounds help us terminate our procedure with a guarantee on the precision of our value function and, correspondingly, on the optimality of the resulting policy.

Proposition 2 (Convergence of Value Iteration)

(Adapted from Puterman (1994) theorem 6.3.1)

Let v0v_0v0​ be any initial value function, ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 a desired accuracy, and let {vn}\{v_n\}{vn​} be the sequence of value functions generated by value iteration, i.e., vn+1=Lvnv_{n+1} = \Bellman v_nvn+1​=Lvn​ for n≥0n \geq 0n≥0, where L\BellmanL is the Bellman optimality operator. Then:

  1. vnv_nvn​ converges to the optimal value function vγ∗v^*_\gammavγ∗​,

  2. The algorithm terminates in finite time,

  3. The resulting policy πε\pi_\varepsilonπε​ is ε\varepsilonε-optimal, and

  4. When the algorithm terminates, vn+1v_{n+1}vn+1​ is within ε/2\varepsilon/2ε/2 of vγ∗v^*_\gammavγ∗​.

Proof 3

Parts 1 and 2 follow directly from the fact that L\BellmanL is a contraction mapping. Hence, by Banach’s fixed-point theorem, it has a unique fixed point (which is vγ∗v^*_\gammavγ∗​), and repeated application of L\BellmanL will converge to this fixed point. Moreover, this convergence happens at a geometric rate, which ensures that we reach the termination condition in finite time.

To show that the Bellman optimality operator L\BellmanL is a contraction mapping, we need to prove that for any two value functions vvv and uuu:

∥Lv−Lu∥∞≤γ∥v−u∥∞\|\Bellman v - \Bellman u\|_\infty \leq \gamma \|v - u\|_\infty∥Lv−Lu∥∞​≤γ∥v−u∥∞​
(63)

where γ∈[0,1)\gamma \in [0,1)γ∈[0,1) is the discount factor and ∥⋅∥∞\|\cdot\|_\infty∥⋅∥∞​ is the supremum norm.

Let’s start by writing out the definition of Lv\Bellman vLv and Lu\Bellman uLu:

(Lv)(s)=max⁡a∈A{r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)v(j)}(Lu)(s)=max⁡a∈A{r(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)u(j)}\begin{align*} (\Bellman v)(s) &= \max_{a \in A} \left\{r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a)v(j)\right\}\\ (\Bellman u)(s) &= \max_{a \in A} \left\{r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a)u(j)\right\} \end{align*}(Lv)(s)(Lu)(s)​=a∈Amax​⎩⎨⎧​r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j)⎭⎬⎫​=a∈Amax​⎩⎨⎧​r(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)u(j)⎭⎬⎫​​
(64)

For any state sss, let ava_vav​ be the action that achieves the maximum for (Lv)(s)(\Bellman v)(s)(Lv)(s), and aua_uau​ be the action that achieves the maximum for (Lu)(s)(\Bellman u)(s)(Lu)(s). By the definition of these maximizers:

(Lv)(s)≥r(s,au)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,au)v(j)(Lu)(s)≥r(s,av)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,av)u(j)\begin{align*} (\Bellman v)(s) &\geq r(s,a_u) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a_u)v(j)\\ (\Bellman u)(s) &\geq r(s,a_v) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a_v)u(j) \end{align*}(Lv)(s)(Lu)(s)​≥r(s,au​)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,au​)v(j)≥r(s,av​)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,av​)u(j)​
(65)

Subtracting these inequalities:

(Lv)(s)−(Lu)(s)≤γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,av)(v(j)−u(j))(Lu)(s)−(Lv)(s)≤γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,au)(u(j)−v(j))\begin{align*} (\Bellman v)(s) - (\Bellman u)(s) &\leq \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a_v)(v(j) - u(j))\\ (\Bellman u)(s) - (\Bellman v)(s) &\leq \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a_u)(u(j) - v(j)) \end{align*}(Lv)(s)−(Lu)(s)(Lu)(s)−(Lv)(s)​≤γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,av​)(v(j)−u(j))≤γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,au​)(u(j)−v(j))​
(66)

Taking the absolute value and using the fact that ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a)=1\sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) = 1∑j∈S​p(j∣s,a)=1:

∣(Lv)(s)−(Lu)(s)∣≤γmax⁡j∈S∣v(j)−u(j)∣=γ∥v−u∥∞|(\Bellman v)(s) - (\Bellman u)(s)| \leq \gamma \max_{j \in \mathcal{S}} |v(j) - u(j)| = \gamma \|v - u\|_\infty∣(Lv)(s)−(Lu)(s)∣≤γj∈Smax​∣v(j)−u(j)∣=γ∥v−u∥∞​
(67)

Since this holds for all s∈Ss \in \mathcal{S}s∈S, taking the supremum over sss gives:

∥Lv−Lu∥∞≤γ∥v−u∥∞\|\Bellman v - \Bellman u\|_\infty \leq \gamma \|v - u\|_\infty∥Lv−Lu∥∞​≤γ∥v−u∥∞​
(68)

Thus, L\BellmanL is a contraction mapping with contraction factor γ\gammaγ.

Now, let’s prove parts 3 and 4. Suppose the algorithm has just terminated, i.e., ∥vn+1−vn∥∞<ε(1−γ)2γ\|v_{n+1} - v_n\|_\infty < \frac{\varepsilon(1-\gamma)}{2\gamma}∥vn+1​−vn​∥∞​<2γε(1−γ)​ for some nnn. We want to show that our current value function vn+1v_{n+1}vn+1​ and the policy πε\pi_\varepsilonπε​ derived from it are close to optimal.

By the triangle inequality:

∥vγπε−vγ∗∥∞≤∥vγπε−vn+1∥∞+∥vn+1−vγ∗∥∞\|v^{\pi_\varepsilon}_\gamma - v^*_\gamma\|_\infty \leq \|v^{\pi_\varepsilon}_\gamma - v_{n+1}\|_\infty + \|v_{n+1} - v^*_\gamma\|_\infty∥vγπε​​−vγ∗​∥∞​≤∥vγπε​​−vn+1​∥∞​+∥vn+1​−vγ∗​∥∞​
(69)

For the first term, since vγπεv^{\pi_\varepsilon}_\gammavγπε​​ is the fixed point of Lπε\mathrm{L}_{\pi_\varepsilon}Lπε​​ and πε\pi_\varepsilonπε​ is greedy with respect to vn+1v_{n+1}vn+1​ (i.e., Lπεvn+1=Lvn+1\mathrm{L}_{\pi_\varepsilon}v_{n+1} = \Bellman v_{n+1}Lπε​​vn+1​=Lvn+1​):

∥vγπε−vn+1∥∞=∥Lπεvγπε−vn+1∥∞≤∥Lπεvγπε−Lπεvn+1∥∞+∥Lπεvn+1−vn+1∥∞=∥Lπεvγπε−Lπεvn+1∥∞+∥Lvn+1−vn+1∥∞≤γ∥vγπε−vn+1∥∞+γ∥vn+1−vn∥∞\begin{aligned} \|v^{\pi_\varepsilon}_\gamma - v_{n+1}\|_\infty &= \|\mathrm{L}_{\pi_\varepsilon}v^{\pi_\varepsilon}_\gamma - v_{n+1}\|_\infty \\ &\leq \|\mathrm{L}_{\pi_\varepsilon}v^{\pi_\varepsilon}_\gamma - \mathrm{L}_{\pi_\varepsilon}v_{n+1}\|_\infty + \|\mathrm{L}_{\pi_\varepsilon}v_{n+1} - v_{n+1}\|_\infty \\ &= \|\mathrm{L}_{\pi_\varepsilon}v^{\pi_\varepsilon}_\gamma - \mathrm{L}_{\pi_\varepsilon}v_{n+1}\|_\infty + \|\Bellman v_{n+1} - v_{n+1}\|_\infty \\ &\leq \gamma\|v^{\pi_\varepsilon}_\gamma - v_{n+1}\|_\infty + \gamma\|v_{n+1} - v_n\|_\infty \end{aligned}∥vγπε​​−vn+1​∥∞​​=∥Lπε​​vγπε​​−vn+1​∥∞​≤∥Lπε​​vγπε​​−Lπε​​vn+1​∥∞​+∥Lπε​​vn+1​−vn+1​∥∞​=∥Lπε​​vγπε​​−Lπε​​vn+1​∥∞​+∥Lvn+1​−vn+1​∥∞​≤γ∥vγπε​​−vn+1​∥∞​+γ∥vn+1​−vn​∥∞​​
(70)

where we used that both L\BellmanL and Lπε\mathrm{L}_{\pi_\varepsilon}Lπε​​ are contractions with factor γ\gammaγ, and that vn+1=Lvnv_{n+1} = \Bellman v_nvn+1​=Lvn​.

Rearranging:

∥vγπε−vn+1∥∞≤γ1−γ∥vn+1−vn∥∞\|v^{\pi_\varepsilon}_\gamma - v_{n+1}\|_\infty \leq \frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\|v_{n+1} - v_n\|_\infty∥vγπε​​−vn+1​∥∞​≤1−γγ​∥vn+1​−vn​∥∞​

Similarly, since vγ∗v^*_\gammavγ∗​ is the fixed point of L\BellmanL:

∥vn+1−vγ∗∥∞=∥Lvn−Lvγ∗∥∞≤γ∥vn−vγ∗∥∞≤γ1−γ∥vn+1−vn∥∞\|v_{n+1} - v^*_\gamma\|_\infty = \|\Bellman v_n - \Bellman v^*_\gamma\|_\infty \leq \gamma\|v_n - v^*_\gamma\|_\infty \leq \frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\|v_{n+1} - v_n\|_\infty∥vn+1​−vγ∗​∥∞​=∥Lvn​−Lvγ∗​∥∞​≤γ∥vn​−vγ∗​∥∞​≤1−γγ​∥vn+1​−vn​∥∞​
(72)

Since ∥vn+1−vn∥∞<ε(1−γ)2γ\|v_{n+1} - v_n\|_\infty < \frac{\varepsilon(1-\gamma)}{2\gamma}∥vn+1​−vn​∥∞​<2γε(1−γ)​:

∥vγπε−vn+1∥∞≤γ1−γ⋅ε(1−γ)2γ=ε2\|v^{\pi_\varepsilon}_\gamma - v_{n+1}\|_\infty \leq \frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma} \cdot \frac{\varepsilon(1-\gamma)}{2\gamma} = \frac{\varepsilon}{2}∥vγπε​​−vn+1​∥∞​≤1−γγ​⋅2γε(1−γ)​=2ε​

∥vn+1−vγ∗∥∞≤γ1−γ⋅ε(1−γ)2γ=ε2\|v_{n+1} - v^*_\gamma\|_\infty \leq \frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma} \cdot \frac{\varepsilon(1-\gamma)}{2\gamma} = \frac{\varepsilon}{2}∥vn+1​−vγ∗​∥∞​≤1−γγ​⋅2γε(1−γ)​=2ε​

∥vγπε−vγ∗∥∞≤ε2+ε2=ε\|v^{\pi_\varepsilon}_\gamma - v^*_\gamma\|_\infty \leq \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon∥vγπε​​−vγ∗​∥∞​≤2ε​+2ε​=ε
(75)

This completes the proof, showing that vn+1v_{n+1}vn+1​ is within ε/2\varepsilon/2ε/2 of vγ∗v^*_\gammavγ∗​ (part 4) and πε\pi_\varepsilonπε​ is ε\varepsilonε-optimal (part 3).

Exact Scheduling MDP for Inference Serving¶

How can a large request-level system be reduced to a finite MDP, and which predictive distinctions disappear in that reduction?

The inference examples have so far treated the scheduling rule as fixed and the GPU clock as the action. In a different decision interface, the clock is fixed and the action is the phase that receives the next unit of service. Prefill admits new requests into decode and consumes cache; decode advances requests already producing output tokens. Serving either phase delays the other.

An exact request-level Markov state would contain every prompt length, generated token count, cache allocation, and waiting time. For computation, these quantities are aggregated into the finite state

s=(p,d,a)∈{0,…,6}2×{0,…,4},s=(p,d,a)\in\{0,\ldots,6\}^2\times\{0,\ldots,4\},s=(p,d,a)∈{0,…,6}2×{0,…,4},
(76)

where ppp counts waiting prefill jobs, ddd counts active decode jobs, and aaa is the oldest prefill-age bin. The actions are

A={prefill,decode,idle}.\mathcal A=\{\text{prefill},\text{decode},\text{idle}\}.A={prefill,decode,idle}.
(77)

An action is masked when its phase is empty. Prefill is also masked at d=6d=6d=6, which represents the cache limit in this abstraction. A Bernoulli arrival probability for each 0.1-second decision period is calibrated from the load-normalized version of the same five-minute Azure trace used in the modeling chapter.

The phase rates and powers come from one measured NVIDIA L4 run of Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct served by vLLM 0.28.0. The reduced MDP uses the 1,125 MHz requested clock level; its batch-balanced median realized graphics clock was 939.375 MHz. The measured prefill rate and the trace’s mean prompt length determine the Bernoulli probability that a prefill action completes one aggregate prompt. A successful completion moves that job into decode. The measured decode rate and mean output length similarly determine one aggregate expected completion budget per decode action. That budget is shared symmetrically across the active jobs, so adding jobs does not multiply the model’s expected completion capacity. Queue counts are capped at six, and arrivals beyond that cap are recorded as drops. These choices define a complete transition matrix Pss′uP_{ss'}^uPss′u​ on 245 states.

The one-step cost assigns separate penalties to congestion, old prompt work, decode stalls, dropped requests, and energy:

c(s,u)=p+d+41{a=4}+2d1{u≠decode}+10E[Ndrop∣s,u]+0.1E(u)Emax⁡.c(s,u)=p+d+4\mathbf 1\{a=4\} +2d\mathbf 1\{u\ne\text{decode}\} +10\mathbb E[N_{\mathrm{drop}}\mid s,u] +0.1\frac{E(u)}{E_{\max}}.c(s,u)=p+d+41{a=4}+2d1{u=decode}+10E[Ndrop​∣s,u]+0.1Emax​E(u)​.
(78)

For prefill, decode, and idle, respectively, the measured profile gives E(u)=(6.427,6.274,2.339)E(u)=(6.427,6.274,2.339)E(u)=(6.427,6.274,2.339) joules per decision period. Each value is the measured phase-power summary at the requested 1,125 MHz level multiplied by 0.1 seconds, rather than a direct request-level energy measurement. Only the ratio E(u)/Emax⁡E(u)/E_{\max}E(u)/Emax​ enters the stage cost.

With γ=0.99\gamma=0.99γ=0.99, cost-minimizing value iteration applies

Qn(s,u)=c(s,u)+γ∑s′Pss′uVn(s′),Vn+1(s)=min⁡u∈A(s)Qn(s,u).\begin{aligned} Q_n(s,u)&=c(s,u)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P_{ss'}^uV_n(s'),\\ V_{n+1}(s)&=\min_{u\in\mathcal A(s)}Q_n(s,u). \end{aligned}Qn​(s,u)Vn+1​(s)​=c(s,u)+γs′∑​Pss′u​Vn​(s′),=u∈A(s)min​Qn​(s,u).​
(79)

Iteration stops when ∥Vn+1−Vn∥∞<10−10\lVert V_{n+1}-V_n\rVert_\infty<10^{-10}∥Vn+1​−Vn​∥∞​<10−10. The final Bellman residual is checked independently and must be below 10-8.

Policy slices compare the optimal phase decision across the two queue lengths and the age of the oldest prompt. A replay applies the resulting policy to fixed evaluation episodes and compares it with the decode-priority rule.

The reduced scheduling MDP has the following transition parameters and value-iteration certificate. The Bellman residual applies only to this finite model.

dp_row = pd.read_csv("artifacts/inference_serving/metrics_dp.csv").iloc[0]
pd.DataFrame(

Download the dynamic-programming certificate (CSV)

Value iteration required 2,454 sweeps on this high-discount problem. Its independently recomputed Bellman residual is 9.823×10−119.823\times10^{-11}9.823×10−11, below both the 10-8 acceptance threshold and the 10-10 stopping tolerance. The certificate concerns the supplied 245-state transition matrix. The optimal policy serves decode whenever d>0d>0d>0, serves prefill when d=0d=0d=0 and p>0p>0p>0, and idles only in the empty state. The same rule appears in all five age slices. For this calibration, the decode-stall penalty and aggregate completion budget make the transparent decode-priority heuristic exactly optimal within the reduced model. A richer state or a different cost can produce a switching boundary instead.

The result is exact for the stated finite MDP, not for vLLM. Aggregating request ages and lengths removes distinctions that can affect head-of-line waiting and cache release. The calibrated transition kernel is stationary, the clock is fixed, temperature is absent from the state, and the action set excludes mixed prefill-decode batches. Measurements from one L4 deployment calibrate the phase rates and powers; they do not establish scheduling performance across L4 systems. The request-level replay from the earlier chapters remains a model-audit tool, not part of the optimality proof.

def solve_scheduling_mdp(
    mdp: SchedulingMDP | None = None,
    *,
    tolerance: float = 1e-10,
    maximum_iterations: int = 100_000,
) -> DPSolution:
    """Solve the reduced discounted scheduling model by value iteration."""

    model = make_scheduling_mdp() if mdp is None else mdp
    model.validate()
    if tolerance <= 0.0 or maximum_iterations <= 0:
        raise ValueError("tolerance and maximum_iterations must be positive")
    value = np.zeros(model.states.shape[0], dtype=float)
    iterations = 0
    for iterations in range(1, maximum_iterations + 1):
        continuation = np.einsum("sak,k->sa", model.transitions, value)
        q_values = model.stage_cost + model.gamma * continuation
        q_values = np.where(model.valid_actions, q_values, np.inf)
        updated = np.min(q_values, axis=1)
        if np.max(np.abs(updated - value)) <= tolerance:
            value = updated
            break
        value = updated
    continuation = np.einsum("sak,k->sa", model.transitions, value)
    q_values = np.where(
        model.valid_actions,
        model.stage_cost + model.gamma * continuation,
        np.inf,
    )
    bellman_update = np.min(q_values, axis=1)
    residual = float(np.max(np.abs(bellman_update - value)))
    policy = np.argmin(q_values, axis=1).astype(int)
    labels = tuple(SCHEDULING_ACTIONS[int(action)] for action in policy)
    return DPSolution(
        value=value,
        policy=policy,
        policy_labels=labels,
        iterations=iterations,
        bellman_residual=residual,
        mdp=model,
    )

Newton-Kantorovich Applied to Bellman Optimality¶

We now apply the Newton-Kantorovich framework to the Bellman optimality equation. Let

(Lv)(s)=max⁡a∈A(s){r(s,a)+γ∑s′p(s′∣s,a)v(s′)}.(\Bellman v)(s) = \max_{a \in A(s)} \left\{ r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} p(s' \mid s,a) v(s') \right\}.(Lv)(s)=a∈A(s)max​{r(s,a)+γs′∑​p(s′∣s,a)v(s′)}.
(80)

The problem is to find vvv such that Lv=v\Bellman v = vLv=v, or equivalently B(v):=Lv−v=0\mathrm{B}(v) := \Bellman v - v = 0B(v):=Lv−v=0. The operator L\BellmanL is piecewise affine, hence not globally differentiable, but it is directionally differentiable everywhere in the Hadamard sense and Fréchet differentiable at points where the maximizer is unique.

We consider three complementary perspectives for understanding and computing its derivative.

Perspective 1: Max of Affine Maps¶

In tabular form, for finite state and action spaces, the Bellman operator can be written as a pointwise maximum of affine maps:

(Lv)(s)=max⁡a∈A(s){r(s,a)+γ(Pav)(s)},(\Bellman v)(s) = \max_{a \in A(s)} \left\{ r(s,a) + \gamma (P_a v)(s) \right\},(Lv)(s)=a∈A(s)max​{r(s,a)+γ(Pa​v)(s)},
(81)

where Pa∈R∣S∣×∣S∣P_a \in \mathbb{R}^{|S| \times |S|}Pa​∈R∣S∣×∣S∣ is the transition matrix associated with action aaa. Each Qav:=ra+γPavQ_a v := r^a + \gamma P_a vQa​v:=ra+γPa​v is affine in vvv. The operator L\BellmanL therefore computes the upper envelope of a finite set of affine functions at each state.

At any vvv, let the active set at state sss be

A∗(s;v):=arg⁡max⁡a∈A(s)(Qav)(s).\mathcal{A}^*(s; v) := \arg\max_{a \in A(s)} (Q_a v)(s).A∗(s;v):=arga∈A(s)max​(Qa​v)(s).
(82)

Then the Hadamard directional derivative exists and is given by

(L′(v;h))(s)=max⁡a∈A∗(s;v)γ(Pah)(s).(\Bellman '(v; h))(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}^*(s; v)} \gamma (P_a h)(s).(L′(v;h))(s)=a∈A∗(s;v)max​γ(Pa​h)(s).
(83)

If the active set is a singleton, this expression becomes linear in hhh, and L\BellmanL is Fréchet differentiable at vvv, with

L′(v)=γPπv,\Bellman'(v) = \gamma P_{\pi_v},L′(v)=γPπv​​,
(84)

where πv(s):=a∗(s)\pi_v(s) := a^*(s)πv​(s):=a∗(s) is the greedy policy at vvv.

Perspective 2: Envelope Theorem¶

Consider now a value function approximated as a linear combination of basis functions:

vc(s)=∑jcjϕj(s).v_c(s) = \sum_j c_j \phi_j(s).vc​(s)=j∑​cj​ϕj​(s).
(85)

At a node sis_isi​, define the parametric maximization

vi(c):=(Lvc)(si)=max⁡a∈A(si){r(si,a)+γ∑jcjEs′∣si,a[ϕj(s′)]}.v_i(c) := (\Bellman v_c)(s_i) = \max_{a \in A(s_i)} \left\{ r(s_i,a) + \gamma \sum_j c_j \mathbb{E}_{s' \mid s_i, a}[\phi_j(s')] \right\}.vi​(c):=(Lvc​)(si​)=a∈A(si​)max​{r(si​,a)+γj∑​cj​Es′∣si​,a​[ϕj​(s′)]}.
(86)

Define

Fi(a,c):=r(si,a)+γ∑jcjEs′∣si,a[ϕj(s′)],F_i(a, c) := r(s_i,a) + \gamma \sum_j c_j \mathbb{E}_{s' \mid s_i, a}[\phi_j(s')],Fi​(a,c):=r(si​,a)+γj∑​cj​Es′∣si​,a​[ϕj​(s′)],
(87)

so that vi(c)=max⁡aFi(a,c)v_i(c) = \max_a F_i(a, c)vi​(c)=maxa​Fi​(a,c). Since FiF_iFi​ is linear in ccc, we can apply the envelope theorem (Danskin’s theorem): if the optimizer ai∗(c)a_i^*(c)ai∗​(c) is unique or selected measurably, then

∂vi∂cj(c)=γEs′∣si,ai∗(c)[ϕj(s′)].\frac{\partial v_i}{\partial c_j}(c) = \gamma \mathbb{E}_{s' \mid s_i, a_i^*(c)}[\phi_j(s')].∂cj​∂vi​​(c)=γEs′∣si​,ai∗​(c)​[ϕj​(s′)].
(88)

We do not need to differentiate the optimizer ai∗(c)a_i^*(c)ai∗​(c) itself. The result extends to the subdifferential case when ties occur, where the Jacobian becomes set-valued.

This result is useful when solving the collocation equation Φc=v(c)\Phi c = v(c)Φc=v(c). Newton’s method requires the Jacobian v′(c)v'(c)v′(c), and this expression allows us to compute it without involving any derivatives of the optimal action.

Perspective 3: The Implicit Function Theorem¶

The third perspective applies the implicit function theorem to understand when the Bellman operator is differentiable despite containing a max operator. The maximization problem defines an implicit relationship between the value function and the optimal action, and the implicit function theorem tells us when this relationship is smooth enough to differentiate through.

The Bellman operator is defined as

(Lv)(s)=max⁡a{r(s,a)+γ∑jp(j∣s,a)v(j)}.(\Bellman v)(s) = \max_{a} \left\{ r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_j p(j \mid s,a) v(j) \right\}.(Lv)(s)=amax​{r(s,a)+γj∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j)}.
(89)

The difficulty is that the max operator encodes a discrete selection: which action achieves the maximum. To apply the implicit function theorem, we reformulate this as follows. For each action aaa, define the action-value function:

Qa(v,s):=r(s,a)+γ∑jp(j∣s,a)v(j).Q_a(v, s) := r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_j p(j \mid s,a) v(j).Qa​(v,s):=r(s,a)+γj∑​p(j∣s,a)v(j).
(90)

The optimal action at vvv satisfies the optimality condition:

Qa∗(s)(v,s)≥Qa(v,s)for all a.Q_{a^*(s)}(v, s) \geq Q_a(v, s) \quad \text{for all } a.Qa∗(s)​(v,s)≥Qa​(v,s)for all a.
(91)

Now suppose that at a particular vvv, action a∗(s)a^*(s)a∗(s) is a strict local maximizer in the sense that there exists δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 such that

Qa∗(s)(v,s)>Qa(v,s)+δfor all a≠a∗(s).Q_{a^*(s)}(v, s) > Q_a(v, s) + \delta \quad \text{for all } a \neq a^*(s).Qa∗(s)​(v,s)>Qa​(v,s)+δfor all a=a∗(s).
(92)

This strict inequality is the regularity condition needed for the implicit function theorem. It ensures that the optimal action is unique at vvv and remains so in a neighborhood of vvv.

To see why, consider any perturbation v+hv + hv+h with ∥h∥\|h\|∥h∥ small. Since QaQ_aQa​ is linear in vvv, we have:

Qa(v+h,s)=Qa(v,s)+γ∑jp(j∣s,a)h(j).Q_a(v+h, s) = Q_a(v, s) + \gamma \sum_j p(j \mid s,a) h(j).Qa​(v+h,s)=Qa​(v,s)+γj∑​p(j∣s,a)h(j).
(93)

The perturbation term is bounded: ∣γ∑jp(j∣s,a)h(j)∣≤γ∥h∥|\gamma \sum_j p(j \mid s,a) h(j)| \leq \gamma \|h\|∣γ∑j​p(j∣s,a)h(j)∣≤γ∥h∥. Therefore, for ∥h∥<δ/γ\|h\| < \delta/\gamma∥h∥<δ/γ, the strict gap ensures that

Qa∗(s)(v+h,s)>Qa(v+h,s)for all a≠a∗(s).Q_{a^*(s)}(v+h, s) > Q_a(v+h, s) \quad \text{for all } a \neq a^*(s).Qa∗(s)​(v+h,s)>Qa​(v+h,s)for all a=a∗(s).
(94)

Thus a∗(s)a^*(s)a∗(s) remains the unique maximizer throughout the neighborhood {v+h:∥h∥<δ/γ}\{v + h : \|h\| < \delta/\gamma\}{v+h:∥h∥<δ/γ}.

The implicit function theorem now applies: in this neighborhood, the mapping v↦a∗(s;v)v \mapsto a^*(s; v)v↦a∗(s;v) is constant (and hence smooth), taking the value a∗(s)a^*(s)a∗(s). This allows us to write

(Lv)(s)=Qa∗(s)(v,s)=r(s,a∗(s))+γ∑jp(j∣s,a∗(s))v(j)(\Bellman v)(s) = Q_{a^*(s)}(v, s) = r(s,a^*(s)) + \gamma \sum_j p(j \mid s,a^*(s)) v(j)(Lv)(s)=Qa∗(s)​(v,s)=r(s,a∗(s))+γj∑​p(j∣s,a∗(s))v(j)
(95)

as an explicit formula that holds throughout the neighborhood. Since Qa∗(s)(⋅,s)Q_{a^*(s)}(\cdot, s)Qa∗(s)​(⋅,s) is an affine (hence smooth) function of vvv, we can differentiate it:

ddv(Lv)(s)=γPa∗(s).\frac{d}{dv} (\Bellman v)(s) = \gamma P_{a^*(s)}.dvd​(Lv)(s)=γPa∗(s)​.
(96)

More precisely, for any perturbation hhh:

(L(v+h))(s)=(Lv)(s)+γ∑jp(j∣s,a∗(s))h(j)+o(∥h∥).(\Bellman (v+h))(s) = (\Bellman v)(s) + \gamma \sum_j p(j \mid s,a^*(s)) h(j) + o(\|h\|).(L(v+h))(s)=(Lv)(s)+γj∑​p(j∣s,a∗(s))h(j)+o(∥h∥).
(97)

This is the Fréchet derivative:

L′(v)=γPπv,\Bellman'(v) = \gamma P_{\pi_v},L′(v)=γPπv​​,
(98)

where πv(s)=a∗(s)\pi_v(s) = a^*(s)πv​(s)=a∗(s) is the greedy policy.

The role of the implicit function theorem: It guarantees that when the maximizer is unique with a strict gap (the regularity condition), the argmax function v↦a∗(s;v)v \mapsto a^*(s; v)v↦a∗(s;v) is locally constant, which removes the non-differentiability of the max operator. Without this regularity condition (specifically, at points where multiple actions tie for optimality), the implicit function theorem does not apply, and the operator is not Fréchet differentiable. The active set perspective (Perspective 1) and the envelope theorem (Perspective 2) provide the tools to handle these non-smooth points.

Connection to Policy Iteration¶

We return to the Newton-Kantorovich step:

(I−L′(vn))hn=vn−Lvn,vn+1=vn−hn.(I - \Bellman'(v_n)) h_n = v_n - \Bellman v_n, \quad v_{n+1} = v_n - h_n.(I−L′(vn​))hn​=vn​−Lvn​,vn+1​=vn​−hn​.
(99)

Suppose L′(vn)=γPπvn\Bellman'(v_n) = \gamma P_{\pi_{v_n}}L′(vn​)=γPπvn​​​ for the greedy policy πvn\pi_{v_n}πvn​​. Then

(I−γPπvn)vn+1=rπvn,(I - \gamma P_{\pi_{v_n}}) v_{n+1} = r^{\pi_{v_n}},(I−γPπvn​​​)vn+1​=rπvn​​,
(100)

which is exactly policy evaluation for πvn\pi_{v_n}πvn​​. Recomputing the greedy policy from vn+1v_{n+1}vn+1​ yields the next iterate.

Thus, policy iteration is Newton-Kantorovich applied to the Bellman optimality equation. At points of nondifferentiability (when ties occur), the operator is still semismooth, and policy iteration corresponds to a semismooth Newton method. The envelope theorem is what justifies the simplification of the Jacobian to γPπv\gamma P_{\pi_v}γPπv​​, bypassing the need to differentiate through the optimizer. This completes the equivalence.

The Semismooth Newton Perspective¶

The three perspectives we developed above (the active set view, the envelope theorem, and the implicit function theorem) all point toward a deeper framework for understanding Newton-type methods on non-smooth operators. This framework, known as semismooth Newton methods, was developed precisely to handle operators like the Bellman operator that are piecewise smooth but not globally differentiable. The connection between policy iteration and semismooth Newton methods has been rigorously developed in recent work Gargiani et al. (2022).

The classical Newton-Kantorovich method assumes the operator is Fréchet differentiable everywhere. The derivative exists, is unique, and varies continuously with the base point. But the Bellman operator L\BellmanL violates this assumption at any value function where multiple actions tie for optimality at some state. At such points, the implicit function theorem fails, and there is no unique Fréchet derivative.

Semismooth Newton methods address this by replacing the notion of a single Jacobian with a generalized derivative that captures the behavior of the operator near non-smooth points. The most commonly used generalized derivative is the Clarke subdifferential, which we can think of as the convex hull of all possible “candidate Jacobians” that arise from limits approaching the non-smooth point from different directions.

For the Bellman residual B(v)=Lv−v\mathrm{B}(v) = \Bellman v - vB(v)=Lv−v, the Clarke subdifferential at a point vvv can be characterized explicitly using our first perspective. Recall that at each state sss, we defined the active set A∗(s;v)=arg⁡max⁡aQa(v,s)\mathcal{A}^*(s; v) = \arg\max_a Q_a(v, s)A∗(s;v)=argmaxa​Qa​(v,s). When this set contains multiple actions, the operator is not Fréchet differentiable. However, it remains directionally differentiable in all directions, and the Clarke subdifferential consists of all matrices of the form

∂B(v)={I−γPπ:π(s)∈A∗(s;v) for all s}.\partial \mathrm{B}(v) = \left\{ I - \gamma P_\pi : \pi(s) \in \mathcal{A}^*(s; v) \text{ for all } s \right\}.∂B(v)={I−γPπ​:π(s)∈A∗(s;v) for all s}.
(101)

In words, the generalized Jacobian is the set of all matrices I−γPπI - \gamma P_\piI−γPπ​ where π\piπ is any policy that selects an action from the active set at each state. When the maximizer is unique everywhere, this set reduces to a singleton, and we recover the classical Fréchet derivative. When ties occur, the set has multiple elements: precisely the convex combinations mentioned in Perspective 1.

The semismooth Newton method for solving B(v)=0\mathrm{B}(v) = 0B(v)=0 proceeds by selecting an element Jk∈∂B(vk)J_k \in \partial \mathrm{B}(v_k)Jk​∈∂B(vk​) at each iteration and solving

Jkhk=−B(vk),vk+1=vk+hk.J_k h_k = -\mathrm{B}(v_k), \quad v_{k+1} = v_k + h_k.Jk​hk​=−B(vk​),vk+1​=vk​+hk​.
(102)

What this tells us is that any choice from the Clarke subdifferential yields a valid Newton-like update. In the context of the Bellman equation, choosing Jk=I−γPπkJ_k = I - \gamma P_{\pi_k}Jk​=I−γPπk​​ where πk\pi_kπk​ is any greedy policy corresponds exactly to the policy evaluation step in policy iteration. The freedom in selecting which action to choose when ties occur translates to the freedom in selecting which element of the subdifferential to use.

Under appropriate regularity conditions (specifically, when the residual function is BD-regular or CD-regular), the semismooth Newton method converges locally at a quadratic rate Gargiani et al. (2022). This means that near the solution, the error decreases quadratically:

∥vk+1−v∗∥≤C∥vk−v∗∥2.\|v_{k+1} - v^*\| \leq C \|v_k - v^*\|^2.∥vk+1​−v∗∥≤C∥vk​−v∗∥2.
(103)

This theoretical result explains an empirical observation that has long been noted in practice: policy iteration typically converges in very few iterations, often just a handful, even when the state and action spaces are enormous and the space of possible policies is exponentially large.

The semismooth Newton framework also suggests a spectrum of methods interpolating between value iteration and policy iteration. Value iteration can be interpreted as a Newton-like method where we choose Jk=IJ_k = IJk​=I at every iteration, ignoring the dependence of L\BellmanL on vvv entirely. This choice guarantees global convergence through the contraction property but sacrifices the quadratic local convergence rate. Policy iteration, at the other extreme, uses the full generalized Jacobian Jk=I−γPπkJ_k = I - \gamma P_{\pi_k}Jk​=I−γPπk​​, achieving quadratic convergence but at the cost of solving a linear system at each iteration.

Between these extremes lie methods that use approximate Jacobians. One natural variant is to choose Jk=αIJ_k = \alpha IJk​=αI for some scalar α>0\alpha > 0α>0. This leads to the update

vk+1=α−1αvk+1αLvk.v_{k+1} = \frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} v_k + \frac{1}{\alpha} \Bellman v_k.vk+1​=αα−1​vk​+α1​Lvk​.
(104)

This is relaxed value iteration with step size 1/α1/\alpha1/α. Taking α>1\alpha > 1α>1 damps the step: the update remains a global contraction, but with the larger modulus 1−(1−γ)/α1 - (1-\gamma)/\alpha1−(1−γ)/α, so it is slower than standard value iteration. Taking α<1\alpha < 1α<1 lengthens the step, which is over-relaxation. The sup-norm argument then gives a contraction only for α>(1+γ)/2\alpha > (1+\gamma)/2α>(1+γ)/2, with modulus (1+γ)/α−1(1+\gamma)/\alpha - 1(1+γ)/α−1, which exceeds γ\gammaγ. Near the solution, however, the rate is set by the eigenvalues of γPπ∗\gamma P_{\pi^*}γPπ∗​. The constant mode now contracts at 1−(1−γ)/α<γ1 - (1-\gamma)/\alpha < \gamma1−(1−γ)/α<γ, so over-relaxation is faster whenever Pπ∗P_{\pi^*}Pπ∗​ has no eigenvalues close to -1. For every α\alphaα, the update requires only pointwise operations rather than solving a linear system. The Newton perspective thus unifies existing algorithms and generates new ones by systematically exploring different approximations to the generalized Jacobian.

The connection to semismooth Newton methods places policy iteration within a broader mathematical framework that extends far beyond dynamic programming. Semismooth Newton methods are used in optimization (for complementarity problems and variational inequalities), in PDE-constrained optimization (for problems with control constraints), and in economics (for equilibrium problems). The Bellman equation, viewed through this lens, is simply one instance of a piecewise smooth equation, and the tools developed for such equations apply directly.

Policy Iteration¶

While we derived policy iteration-like steps from the Newton-Kantorovich method, it’s worth examining policy iteration as a standalone algorithm, as it has been traditionally presented in the field of dynamic programming.

The policy iteration algorithm for discounted Markov decision problems is as follows:

Algorithm 3 (Policy Iteration)

Input: MDP (S,A,P,R,γ)(S, A, P, R, \gamma)(S,A,P,R,γ) Output: Optimal policy π∗\pi^*π∗

  1. Initialize: n=0n = 0n=0, select an arbitrary decision rule π0∈ΠMD\pi_0 \in \Pi^{MD}π0​∈ΠMD

  2. repeat 3. (Policy evaluation) Obtain vn\mathbf{v}^nvn by solving:

    (I−γPπn)v=rπn(\mathbf{I}-\gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_n}) \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{r}_{\pi_n}(I−γPπn​​)v=rπn​​
    (105)

    1. (Policy improvement) Choose πn+1=Greedy(vn)\pi_{n+1} = \mathrm{Greedy}(\mathbf{v}^n)πn+1​=Greedy(vn) where:

      πn+1∈arg⁡max⁡π∈ΠMD{rπ+γPπvn}\pi_{n+1} \in \arg\max_{\pi \in \Pi^{MD}}\left\{\mathbf{r}_\pi+\gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi \mathbf{v}^n\right\}πn+1​∈argπ∈ΠMDmax​{rπ​+γPπ​vn}
      (106)

      equivalently, for each sss:

      πn+1(s)∈arg⁡max⁡a∈As{r(s,a)+γ∑jp(j∣s,a)vn(j)}\pi_{n+1}(s) \in \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s}\left\{r(s,a)+\gamma \sum_j p(j|s,a) \mathbf{v}^n(j)\right\}πn+1​(s)∈arga∈As​max​{r(s,a)+γj∑​p(j∣s,a)vn(j)}
      (107)

      Set πn+1=πn\pi_{n+1} = \pi_nπn+1​=πn​ if possible.

    2. If πn+1=πn\pi_{n+1} = \pi_nπn+1​=πn​, return π∗=πn\pi^* = \pi_nπ∗=πn​

    3. n=n+1n = n + 1n=n+1

  3. until convergence

As opposed to value iteration, this algorithm produces a sequence of both deterministic Markovian decision rules {πn}\{\pi_n\}{πn​} and value functions {vn}\{\mathbf{v}^n\}{vn}. We recognize in this algorithm the linearization step of the Newton-Kantorovich procedure, which takes place here in the policy evaluation step 3 where we solve the linear system (I−γPπn)v=rπn(\mathbf{I}-\gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_n}) \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{r}_{\pi_n}(I−γPπn​​)v=rπn​​. In practice, this linear system could be solved either using direct methods (eg. Gaussian elimination), using simple iterative methods such as the successive approximation method for policy evaluation, or more sophisticated methods such as GMRES.

Example: Sailing to a Windward Mark in a Shifting Wind¶

How should a sailor beat to a mark upwind when the wind direction keeps changing, and do the rules of thumb that racing sailors learn on the water follow from the Bellman equation?

A sailboat cannot sail straight into the wind. To reach a mark that lies upwind, it sails at an angle to the wind on one tack, with the wind coming over one side of the boat, and then turns through the wind onto the other tack. The boat is on starboard tack when the wind comes over its right side and on port tack when it comes over its left side. Each change of tack costs time. When the wind shifts, one tack points closer to the mark (it is lifted) and the other points further away (it is headed). Racing sailors are taught to tack when headed and to avoid sailing out to the laylines, the lines from which the mark can be reached on a single tack, too early. Vanderbei (1996) posed this problem as a stochastic dynamic program on a grid. It later became the “sailing” benchmark for online planning in Péret & Garcia (2004), Kocsis & Szepesvári (2006) and Bonet & Geffner (2012), where value iteration supplies the exact optimal values against which sampled planners are scored.

States. The lake is a grid of 21×2121\times 2121×21 waypoints. The state is s=(x,y,w,τ)s=(x,y,w,\tau)s=(x,y,w,τ): the boat’s waypoint (x,y)(x,y)(x,y), with xxx pointing east and yyy north; the direction w∈{N,NE,…,NW}w\in\{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{NE},\ldots,\mathrm{NW}\}w∈{N,NE,…,NW} the wind blows from; and the current tack τ∈{port,starboard}\tau\in\{\text{port},\text{starboard}\}τ∈{port,starboard}. The tack must be part of the state because the cost of the next leg depends on it. There are 212×8×2=705621^2\times 8\times 2=7056212×8×2=7056 states. The start is the waypoint (10,2)(10,2)(10,2) and the mark is (10,18)(10,18)(10,18), 16 rows to the north. The mark is an absorbing state with zero cost.

Actions. Each leg goes to one of the 8 neighbouring waypoints, so the action is a heading a∈{N,NE,…,NW}a\in\{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{NE},\ldots,\mathrm{NW}\}a∈{N,NE,…,NW}. Let θ(w,a)∈{0,45,…,180}\theta(w,a)\in\{0,45,\ldots,180\}θ(w,a)∈{0,45,…,180} be the angle in degrees between the wind direction and the heading. The heading θ=0\theta=0θ=0 points into the wind and is not allowed, and neither is a heading that leaves the lake.

Costs. The cost of a leg is its duration in minutes. Following Vanderbei (1996), a leg between two neighbouring waypoints in a straight line takes t(45)=4t(45)=4t(45)=4 minutes close-hauled, t(90)=3t(90)=3t(90)=3 minutes on a beam reach and t(135)=2t(135)=2t(135)=2 minutes on a broad reach. Dead downwind takes t(180)=1t(180)=1t(180)=1 minute, the default of the benchmark code of Bonet & Geffner (2012). A diagonal leg is 2\sqrt 22​ times longer, and we let it take 2\sqrt 22​ times as long, which reproduces the range of leg costs, 1 to 8.6 minutes, reported by Kocsis & Szepesvári (2006). Let τ′(w,a,τ)\tau'(w,a,\tau)τ′(w,a,τ) be the tack after the leg: starboard if the wind comes from the right of the heading, port if it comes from the left, and unchanged when sailing dead downwind. A change of tack wastes δ=3\delta=3δ=3 minutes Vanderbei, 1996. The cost is

c(s,a)=ℓ(a) t(θ(w,a))+δ 1{τ′(w,a,τ)≠τ},c(s,a)=\ell(a)\,t\big(\theta(w,a)\big)+\delta\,\mathbb 1\{\tau'(w,a,\tau)\neq\tau\},c(s,a)=ℓ(a)t(θ(w,a))+δ1{τ′(w,a,τ)=τ},
(108)

where ℓ(a)=1\ell(a)=1ℓ(a)=1 for N, E, S, W and ℓ(a)=2\ell(a)=\sqrt2ℓ(a)=2​ for the diagonals.

Transitions. The boat moves deterministically to the neighbouring waypoint (x′,y′)(x',y')(x′,y′) in direction aaa. At the end of the leg the wind keeps its direction or shifts by 45∘45^\circ45∘ according to a Markov chain q(w′∣w)q(w'\mid w)q(w′∣w), so

p((x′,y′,w′,τ′)∣s,a)=q(w′∣w).p\big((x',y',w',\tau')\mid s,a\big)=q(w'\mid w).p((x′,y′,w′,τ′)∣s,a)=q(w′∣w).
(109)

We compare three chains. In the steady chain the wind never changes. The oscillating chain uses teaching values for a breeze that swings around north: from north it shifts left or right with probability 0.1 each; from any other direction it moves back towards north with probability 0.2, further away with probability 0.1, and otherwise persists. The shifty chain is the default matrix of the benchmark code of Bonet & Geffner (2012), rotated so that the wind it favours blows from the north. It keeps the wind’s direction with probability 0.2 to 0.4 only.

Objective. The goal is the least expected time to the mark,

v∗(s)=min⁡πEsπ[∑t=0T−1c(St,At)],v^*(s)=\min_\pi \mathbb E^\pi_s\Big[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}c(S_t,A_t)\Big],v∗(s)=πmin​Esπ​[t=0∑T−1​c(St​,At​)],
(110)

where TTT is the first leg that ends at the mark. This is a stochastic shortest-path problem: there is no discount, and the horizon is random because the race ends when the mark is reached. A discount factor would make a minute late in the race cheaper than a minute at the start, which is not what a racer wants, so we keep γ=1\gamma=1γ=1. The Bellman operator

(Lv)(s)=min⁡a∈As{c(s,a)+∑w′q(w′∣w) v(x′,y′,w′,τ′(w,a,τ))}(\Bellman v)(s)=\min_{a\in\mathcal A_s}\Big\{c(s,a)+\sum_{w'}q(w'\mid w)\,v\big(x',y',w',\tau'(w,a,\tau)\big)\Big\}(Lv)(s)=a∈As​min​{c(s,a)+w′∑​q(w′∣w)v(x′,y′,w′,τ′(w,a,τ))}
(111)

is then not a contraction in the sup norm, and the argument of Proposition 2 does not apply. A different argument does. Some policy reaches the mark with probability one (a proper policy), and every leg costs at least one minute, so a policy that fails to reach the mark has infinite expected cost. Under these two conditions Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis (1991) show that v∗v^*v∗ is the unique fixed point of L\BellmanL and that value iteration converges to it from any starting function. We run Algorithm 2 with min⁡\minmin in place of max⁡\maxmax from v0=0v_0=0v0​=0 and stop when ∥vn+1−vn∥∞<10−9\|v_{n+1}-v_n\|_\infty<10^{-9}∥vn+1​−vn​∥∞​<10−9 minutes. We also run Algorithm 3 from a baseline policy described below.

The baseline is a layline sailor who ignores the shifts when deciding where to tack. This sailor stays on starboard tack until reaching the port layline of the mean (north) wind, then sails port tack towards the mark, and does the mirror image on the right side of the course. On each leg the sailor takes the allowed heading on that tack that ends closest to the mark. A second baseline, the certainty-equivalent planner, replans every leg as if the wind it sees now will never change. The table gives the expected time from the start with the wind from the north. All values are exact policy evaluations. For the optimal policy and the layline sailor, the mean of 4000 simulated races per chain agrees with them within four standard errors.

WindOptimal (value iteration)Certainty-equivalentLayline sailorValue-iteration sweepsPolicy-iteration improvements
Steady wind from the north93.593.593.53910
Oscillating breeze (teaching values)84.185.686.6426
Shifty breeze (mdp-engine matrix)72.474.375.2455

Expected time in minutes from the start to the windward mark, 16 rows upwind on a 21 by 21 lake, with the wind from the north at the start. Certainty-equivalent plans each leg as if the wind seen now will never change; the layline sailor tacks only on the laylines of the mean wind. Value iteration starts from zero and stops when the sup-norm residual is below 1e-09 minutes; policy iteration starts from the layline sailor.

In a steady wind the three policies coincide. The best course is one tack, 16 diagonal legs of 424\sqrt242​ minutes plus one 3-minute tack, or 93.5 minutes, and the build script checks that value iteration returns exactly this number. Shifts make the race shorter on average for every policy, because a lifted boat can sail straight north at 4 minutes per row instead of 42≈5.74\sqrt2\approx5.742​≈5.7. The optimal policy uses them best. In the oscillating breeze it needs 84.1 minutes against 86.6 for the layline sailor; in the shifty breeze, 72.4 against 75.2. The gain is about 3% of the race, and it is a gain in expectation. Over 4000 paired races in the oscillating breeze, the optimal boat finishes first in 62% of them and ties in 8%, so the layline sailor still wins about three races in ten. The certainty-equivalent planner sits in between, at 85.6 and 74.3 minutes, so reacting to the wind seen now captures part of the gain and planning for the wind still to come captures the rest.

Two pieces of sailing lore can be read off the policy. The first is tack on the headers. Take the open water below the mark and at least three columns inside both laylines, and look at every state in which the wind has shifted 45∘45^\circ45∘ from north, on either tack. In the oscillating breeze the optimal policy ends the next leg on the lifted tack in all 900 such states; in the shifty breeze it does so in 93% of them. A 45∘45^\circ45∘ header leaves the headed boat sailing across the course with no progress towards the mark, so paying 3 minutes to tack is worth it even though the shift may soon reverse. Panel (b) of Figure 5 shows this as a field of red arrows. The second is stay away from the laylines. In the mean wind a starboard boat eight rows below the mark tacks as soon as it is four columns left of the mark, halfway to the layline (panel (a)). The reason is the one sailors give. On the layline itself, any shift hurts: a header forces an extra tack, and a lift means the boat has sailed further than needed. Staying near the middle of the course keeps both options open. For a planner that assumes the wind seen now will persist, like the certainty-equivalent planner, every tack point inside the laylines is equally good, so nothing pushes it away from them. Neither rule is written into the model; both come out of the minimization in L\BellmanL.

The two algorithms reach v∗v^*v∗ in different ways. Value iteration from v0=0v_0=0v0​=0 computes, at sweep nnn, the least expected cost of nnn legs with no penalty for where the boat ends. For a boat far from the mark, the cheapest nnn legs are cheap reaching and running legs that do not lead to the mark, so vnv_nvn​ stays well below v∗v^*v∗ there. The values settle near the mark first, and the region within one minute of v∗v^*v∗ spreads outwards from the mark until it covers the lake at sweep 37. The value-iteration mode of the replay shows this. The sup-norm error stays above one minute for the first 36 sweeps and then collapses. In the oscillating breeze the residual reaches exactly zero after 42 sweeps. Under the optimal policy every course reaches the mark within 33 legs whatever the wind does, so value iteration ends like backward induction with a horizon of a few dozen legs rather than converging geometrically. Policy iteration started from the layline sailor needs 6 improvement steps. Each step evaluates a whole policy, the linear system of Algorithm 3 (solved here by iterating that policy’s own Bellman operator), and the error falls from 14.4 minutes to zero.

The model is a teaching version of the real problem. Real wind shifts are usually much smaller than 45∘45^\circ45∘, and they happen in time, not at waypoints; the boat’s speed also depends on wind strength, which is fixed here. The leg times and tack delay are the published values of the benchmark, not measurements of any boat, and the oscillating chain, the lake and the two baselines are our choices. No measured sailing data are used. What carries over is the structure: a cost-to-go that depends on the wind as well as the position, a value function that is the unique fixed point of the Bellman operator without any discount, and sailing rules of thumb recovered as properties of the optimal policy.
