Example: Maintaining a Bridge Deck¶

When should a highway agency repair a concrete bridge deck that has not failed yet, and how much does a condition-based rule save over a fixed schedule?

Every highway bridge in the United States is inspected, usually every two years, and the inspector gives the deck a condition rating from 9 (excellent) to 0 (failed). The ratings are reported each year to the National Bridge Inventory (NBI), where the deck rating is item 58. Decks get worse slowly and at random, through cracking, corrosion of the reinforcing steel and spalling. An agency can do nothing, seal and patch the deck, overlay or rehabilitate it, or replace it. Work costs money now; a deck in poor condition costs money later, through the risk of a failure that closes the bridge. The trade-off repeats every year without a natural end, so we model it as an infinite-horizon discounted MDP and solve it with the algorithms of this chapter.

States. The state is the deck rating, observed once a year. Ratings 9 to 5 are kept apart and ratings 4 and below are merged into one poor state, so S={9,8,7,6,5,≤4}\mathcal S=\{9,8,7,6,5,{\le}4\}S={9,8,7,6,5,≤4}. Merging the lowest ratings follows the deck model of Saifullah et al. (2024), whose costs we use below.

Actions. In every state As={nothing,minor,major,replace}\mathcal A_s=\{\text{nothing},\text{minor},\text{major},\text{replace}\}As​={nothing,minor,major,replace}: a minor repair (sealing and patching), a major repair (rehabilitation or an overlay), or a new deck.

Transitions. The do-nothing kernel p(j∣s,nothing)p(j\mid s,\text{nothing})p(j∣s,nothing) is estimated from NBI records by counting. We use the deck histories assembled by Liu et al. (2023), which contain the item-58 rating of 88,596 decks for every year from 1993 to 2019 and are mirrored in their public code repository. No history in that sample ever goes up, so it holds only decks that received no rating-raising work. With nsjn_{sj}nsj​ the number of years in which a deck went from rating sss to rating jjj, the maximum-likelihood estimate is

p^(j∣s,nothing)=nsj∑knsk,\hat p(j\mid s,\text{nothing})=\frac{n_{sj}}{\sum_{k} n_{sk}} ,p^​(j∣s,nothing)=∑k​nsk​nsj​​,
(112)

computed from 2,303,496 year-to-year pairs. The diagonal is large: a deck stays at rating 9 with probability 0.85 per year, at 8 with 0.92, at 7 with 0.97, at 6 with 0.97 and at 5 with 0.98. These correspond to mean stays of 6.5, 12.9, 30.9, 36.4 and 55.7 years. No deck improves without work, so the poor state is absorbing under “nothing”.

The effects of work are teaching assumptions, in the spirit of the component model of Andriotis & Papakonstantinou (2020). Let g(s,a)g(s,a)g(s,a) be the rating right after the work: a minor repair raises the rating by one but cannot fix a poor deck, a major repair raises it by two up to at most 8, and replacement gives a new deck, g(s,replace)=9g(s,\text{replace})=9g(s,replace)=9. The deck then deteriorates for the rest of the year as if nothing had been done:

p(j∣s,a)=p^(j∣g(s,a),nothing).p(j\mid s,a)=\hat p\big(j\mid g(s,a),\text{nothing}\big).p(j∣s,a)=p^​(j∣g(s,a),nothing).
(113)

Costs. Costs are in US dollars per square meter of deck. The work costs are k(nothing)=0k(\text{nothing})=0k(nothing)=0, k(minor)=400k(\text{minor})=400k(minor)=400, k(major)=1,200k(\text{major})=1{,}200k(major)=1,200 and k(replace)=2,650k(\text{replace})=2{,}650k(replace)=2,650, from Table 7 of Saifullah et al. (2024). Their Table 6 gives an annual failure probability q(s)q(s)q(s) of 0.001 for ratings 9 and 8, 0.005 for 7, 6 and 5, and 0.01 for the poor state, and they charge a failure ten times the rebuilding cost. We take F=10×2,650=26,500F=10\times2{,}650=26{,}500F=10×2,650=26,500 and leave out the further cost they accrue while a failed bridge is out of service. The one-period cost is the work cost plus the expected failure cost of the repaired deck,

c(s,a)=k(a)+q(g(s,a)) F.c(s,a)=k(a)+q\big(g(s,a)\big)\,F .c(s,a)=k(a)+q(g(s,a))F.
(114)

A deck left alone thus costs 26.5 per year at ratings 9 and 8, 132.5 at ratings 7 to 5, and 265 when poor.

Discount. We use γ=0.97\gamma=0.97γ=0.97, a 3% annual rate, as Saifullah et al. (2024) do.

The optimal value v⋆(s)v^\star(s)v⋆(s) is the smallest expected discounted cost from rating sss, and it solves the Bellman equation with a minimum in place of the maximum,

v⋆(s)=min⁡a∈As{c(s,a)+γ∑j∈Sp(j∣s,a) v⋆(j)}.v^\star(s)=\min_{a\in\mathcal A_s}\Big\{c(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{j\in\mathcal S}p(j\mid s,a)\,v^\star(j)\Big\}.v⋆(s)=a∈As​min​{c(s,a)+γj∈S∑​p(j∣s,a)v⋆(j)}.
(115)

We solve it twice. Value iteration (Algorithm 2, with a minimum) starts from v0=0v_0=0v0​=0 and stops when ∥vn+1−vn∥∞<ε(1−γ)/(2γ)\lVert v_{n+1}-v_n\rVert_\infty<\varepsilon(1-\gamma)/(2\gamma)∥vn+1​−vn​∥∞​<ε(1−γ)/(2γ) with ε=10−6\varepsilon=10^{-6}ε=10−6 dollars per square meter. With γ=0.97\gamma=0.97γ=0.97 the error shrinks by about 3% per sweep, and the rule is met after 728 sweeps. Policy iteration (Algorithm 3) starts from “do nothing everywhere”, solves the 6×66\times66×6 linear system (I−γPπ)v=cπ(\mathbf I-\gamma\mathbf P_\pi)\mathbf v=\mathbf c_\pi(I−γPπ​)v=cπ​ at each step, and stops after three evaluations. Its second policy already repairs every deck rated 7 or worse; the third changes the action at two ratings and is optimal. This is the Newton behavior described above: a handful of linear solves instead of hundreds of contractions. The two methods return the same policy, and the tests check it against all 46=4,0964^6=4{,}09646=4,096 stationary deterministic policies.

We compare the optimal policy with two rules that need no model. The reactive rule does nothing until the deck is poor and then replaces it. The schedule applies a minor repair every kkk years whatever the rating, and replaces the deck when it is poor; we report the best kkk between 1 and 40. Because the schedule depends on the year, we evaluate it exactly on the Markov chain over the pair (year modulo kkk, rating).

In the base case the optimal policy does nothing at ratings 9 and 8, applies a minor repair at ratings 7, 6 and 5, and a major repair when the deck is poor. It never replaces a deck. The policy is a control limit: work starts at the first rating where the failure risk jumps, from 26.5 to 132.5 dollars per square meter per year, and the work gets heavier as the deck gets worse. A minor repair at rating 7 costs 400 and moves the deck back to 8, which saves about 106 per year for as long as it stays there, a mean of 12.9 years. For a new deck the expected discounted cost is 1,864 dollars per square meter, against 2,951 for the best schedule and 3,200 for the reactive rule.

Failure cost (× replacement)Optimal action at ratings 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, ≤4OptimalBest scheduleReactive
2nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing8921,141 (every 40 yr)1,090
5nothing, nothing, minor, minor, nothing, major1,8412,248 (every 40 yr)2,223
10 (base)nothing, nothing, minor, minor, minor, major2,3113,623 (every 9 yr)4,112
20nothing, nothing, minor, minor, minor, major3,2425,615 (every 6 yr)7,889

Expected discounted cost in USD per m² of deck (γ = 0.97), averaged over the first-year NBI ratings of the decks in the sample. Schedule is a minor repair every k years, with the best k, plus a replacement whenever the deck is poor; reactive does nothing until the deck is poor and then replaces it. Do-nothing transitions: GitHub mirror of NBI records.

The table shows that the answer is driven by the price of failure. When a failure costs only twice the replacement cost, the best policy is never to touch the deck. The poor state then costs 53 per year, and no repair pays for itself at a 3% discount rate. The control limit is not guaranteed either. With a failure cost of five times replacement, the optimal policy repairs decks rated 7 and 6 but leaves decks rated 5 alone. A minor repair moves a deck from 5 to 6, where the failure probability is the same, so it only delays the arrival in the poor state. With a failure cost of 40 times replacement, a deck rated 6 gets a major repair and a deck rated 5 a minor one, for the same reason: a major repair lifts 6 to 8, out of the higher-risk band, while from 5 it would only reach 7. Monotone optimal policies follow from conditions on the costs and transitions Puterman, 1994, and the step-shaped failure table breaks them. In every row the optimal policy beats both rules, and the gap grows with the failure cost, to 3,720 dollars per square meter against the best schedule and 10,344 against the reactive rule at 40 times replacement.

The replay shows the same comparison on sample paths. In the base case, after 50 years the 12 decks under the optimal policy have cost 1,863 dollars per square meter on average, in discounted terms, against 3,196 under the reactive rule and 2,880 under the best schedule. The schedule wastes money on decks that are still rated 9 or 8, while the reactive rule lets decks sit at ratings 7 to 5, where the yearly risk is five times higher, for decades.

Several parts of this model are real and several are not. The do-nothing kernel comes from real inspection records, but it is pooled over all decks regardless of age, traffic, climate and material, and it is estimated from a sample that excludes every deck whose rating went up. Decks that deteriorated fast are the ones most likely to have been repaired, so the mean stays above are probably too long. The work costs and failure probabilities are published values that their authors call indicative, the effects of the repairs are assumptions, and the cost has no term for traffic delays or posting a weight limit. Inspections are treated as exact, while real ratings are noisy, which turns the problem into the partially observed one studied by Andriotis & Papakonstantinou (2020). Finally, an agency manages thousands of decks under one budget, which couples the per-deck problems that we solved separately here.

Example: Controlling an Invasive Plant in a River Network¶

Which stretch of a river should be treated each year to keep an invasive plant in check, and how large can the river get before an exact answer is out of reach?

Tamarisk, or saltcedar, is a shrub that has invaded the banks of many rivers in the western United States. It crowds out native trees such as willows and cottonwoods, and its seeds travel with the water, so an infestation upstream reseeds everything below it. Land managers can kill the plants in a stretch of river, or kill them and plant natives in their place, but each treatment costs money and only part of the network can be treated each year. Hall et al. (2012) formulated this problem as an MDP on a river network, and Alkaee Taleghan et al. (2015) used it as a benchmark for planning with a simulator. We build a small version of their model, solve it exactly with value iteration and policy iteration, and then watch the exact methods run out of room as the river grows.

States. The river is a binary tree of nnn reaches, the stretches of river between two confluences. Water flows from the leaves toward reach 1, the outlet. Each reach has one site for a tree, as in the smallest instances of Alkaee Taleghan et al. (2015), and the site is empty (EEE), holds a native tree (NNN) or holds tamarisk (TTT). The state is s=(s1,…,sn)∈{E,N,T}ns=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\in\{E,N,T\}^ns=(s1​,…,sn​)∈{E,N,T}n, so ∣S∣=3n|\mathcal S|=3^n∣S∣=3n.

Actions. For each reach iii the manager chooses ai∈{0,1,2}a_i\in\{0,1,2\}ai​∈{0,1,2}: do nothing, eradicate, or restore. Eradication kills a tamarisk plant with probability χ=0.85\chi=0.85χ=0.85. Restoration first eradicates and then plants a native tree in the empty site, which takes with probability β=0.65\beta=0.65β=0.65. Without a budget the joint action a=(a1,…,an)a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)a=(a1​,…,an​) ranges over 3n3^n3n choices. With the budget of Alkaee Taleghan et al. (2015), at most one reach is treated per year,

A={a∈{0,1,2}n: ∑i1{ai≠0}≤1},∣A∣=2n+1.\mathcal A=\Big\{a\in\{0,1,2\}^n:\ \textstyle\sum_{i}\mathbf 1\{a_i\neq 0\}\le 1\Big\}, \qquad |\mathcal A| = 2n+1 .A={a∈{0,1,2}n: ∑i​1{ai​=0}≤1},∣A∣=2n+1.
(116)

Then every plant dies with probability 0.2, with kernel δ(zi∣yi)\delta(z_i\mid y_i)δ(zi​∣yi​). Last, the survivors zzz reseed the empty sites. Each surviving plant releases 100 seeds, and a seed from reach kkk lands in reach iii with probability

Kki ∝ 0.5 d(k,i)  0.1 u(k,i),K_{ki}\ \propto\ 0.5^{\,d(k,i)}\;0.1^{\,u(k,i)},Kki​ ∝ 0.5d(k,i)0.1u(k,i),

The values 0.5 and 0.1 are the downstream and upstream dispersal parameters of Alkaee Taleghan et al. (2015); the geometric form is our simplification of the model they cite. Each empty reach also receives on average 1 tamarisk seed and 4 native seeds from outside the network. We treat the seeds that reach iii as Poisson with means

λiT(z)=1+100∑k: zk=TKki,λiN(z)=4+100∑k: zk=NKki.\lambda^T_i(z)=1+100\sum_{k:\,z_k=T}K_{ki},\qquad \lambda^N_i(z)=4+100\sum_{k:\,z_k=N}K_{ki}.λiT​(z)=1+100k:zk​=T∑​Kki​,λiN​(z)=4+100k:zk​=N∑​Kki​.

Otherwise one seed takes it, and tamarisk wins with probability 1.5λiT/(1.5λiT+λiN)1.5\lambda^T_i/(1.5\lambda^T_i+\lambda^N_i)1.5λiT​/(1.5λiT​+λiN​), where 1.5 is one of the values of tamarisk’s competitive advantage examined by Hall et al. (2012). An occupied site keeps its plant. Call gi(ji∣z)g_i(j_i\mid z)gi​(ji​∣z) the resulting distribution of reach iii next year. Given the survivors, the reaches fill independently, so

p(j∣s,a)=∑y,z ∏i=1nαai(yi∣si) ∏i=1nδ(zi∣yi) ∏i=1ngi(ji∣z),Pa=Aa D G,p(j\mid s,a)=\sum_{y,z}\ \prod_{i=1}^n\alpha_{a_i}(y_i\mid s_i)\ \prod_{i=1}^n\delta(z_i\mid y_i)\ \prod_{i=1}^n g_i(j_i\mid z), \qquad \mathbf P_a=\mathbf A_a\,\mathbf D\,\mathbf G ,p(j∣s,a)=y,z∑​ i=1∏n​αai​​(yi​∣si​) i=1∏n​δ(zi​∣yi​) i=1∏n​gi​(ji​∣z),Pa​=Aa​DG,
(119)

with Aa=αa1⊗⋯⊗αan\mathbf A_a=\alpha_{a_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\alpha_{a_n}Aa​=αa1​​⊗⋯⊗αan​​ and D=δ⊗⋯⊗δ\mathbf D=\delta\otimes\cdots\otimes\deltaD=δ⊗⋯⊗δ Kronecker products of 3×33\times 33×3 matrices, and G\mathbf GG a dense 3n×3n3^n\times 3^n3n×3n matrix. The coupling between reaches enters only through G\mathbf GG.

Costs and discount. Following Alkaee Taleghan et al. (2015), each invaded reach costs 1.0 for the damage plus 0.1 for the tamarisk site it holds, and the treatments cost κ=(0, 0.5, 0.9)\kappa=(0,\,0.5,\,0.9)κ=(0,0.5,0.9) for nothing, eradicate and restore:

c(s,a)=1.1∑i=1n1{si=T}+∑i=1nκ(ai),γ=0.9.c(s,a)=1.1\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{s_i=T\}+\sum_{i=1}^n\kappa(a_i), \qquad \gamma=0.9 .c(s,a)=1.1i=1∑n​1{si​=T}+i=1∑n​κ(ai​),γ=0.9.
(120)

The costs are in abstract units. The goal is to minimize the expected discounted cost E[∑t≥0γtc(St,At)]\mathbb E\big[\sum_{t\ge 0}\gamma^t c(S_t,A_t)\big]E[∑t≥0​γtc(St​,At​)].

Solution. Value iteration (Algorithm 2, with a minimum in place of the maximum) computes

vk+1(s)=min⁡a∈A{c(s,a)+γ∑jp(j∣s,a) vk(j)},v_{k+1}(s)=\min_{a\in\mathcal A}\Big\{c(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{j}p(j\mid s,a)\,v_k(j)\Big\},vk+1​(s)=a∈Amin​{c(s,a)+γj∑​p(j∣s,a)vk​(j)},
(121)

and stops when ∥vk+1−vk∥∞<ε(1−γ)/(2γ)\|v_{k+1}-v_k\|_\infty<\varepsilon(1-\gamma)/(2\gamma)∥vk+1​−vk​∥∞​<ε(1−γ)/(2γ) with ε=10−6\varepsilon=10^{-6}ε=10−6. The factored form of Pa\mathbf P_aPa​ means that no transition matrix is ever stored. Each sweep computes w=DGvk\mathbf w=\mathbf D\mathbf G v_kw=DGvk​ once and then applies the small factors of Aa\mathbf A_aAa​ to w\mathbf ww for every action. Policy iteration (Algorithm 3) starts from “do nothing”, solves (I−γPπ)v=cπ(\mathbf I-\gamma\mathbf P_\pi)v=\mathbf c_\pi(I−γPπ​)v=cπ​ exactly at each step, and improves greedily. On the 7-reach river, with 37=2,1873^7=2{,}18737=2,187 states and 15 actions, value iteration stops after 148 sweeps and policy iteration after 4 improvements. The two value functions agree to within 5×10−75\times10^{-7}5×10−7.

Every policy in the table below is evaluated exactly, by solving its policy-evaluation equations, so the numbers are expectations rather than averages of simulated episodes.

Expected discounted cost (γ = 0.9) on the 7-reach river, computed exactly by solving the policy-evaluation equations. The first four policies respect the budget of one treated reach per year; the last two do not. Uniform start averages over all 2187 starting states.

The optimal policy treats some invaded reach in every one of the 2,059 states that contain tamarisk, yet it agrees with the “most upstream first” rule in only 678 of them and with the “most downstream first” rule in 672. From a fully invaded river it restores reach 2, which sits between two headwater reaches and the outlet, rather than a headwater reach or the outlet itself. When a single tamarisk plant stands among natives, it eradicates instead of restoring, because the native seed rain will usually refill the site and the cheaper treatment suffices. These choices lower the expected cost from a fully invaded river from 38.33 under the best heuristic to 36.89, and from 14.53 to 13.30 averaged over all starting states. The budget matters more than the choice of reach. Restoring every invaded reach each year, which the budget forbids, costs 19.83 from a fully invaded river, and the optimal policy without a budget costs 18.98.

The same solvers run on rivers of 1 to 8 reaches (Figure 8). The number of value-iteration sweeps barely changes, from 140 to 150, because it depends on γ\gammaγ and ε\varepsilonε rather than on the size of the model. Policy iteration needs 3 or 4 improvements at every size. What grows is the work per sweep. The states grow as 3n3^n3n, and a dense table of p(j∣s,a)p(j\mid s,a)p(j∣s,a) would hold 9n(2n+1)9^n(2n+1)9n(2n+1) numbers with the budget and 27n27^n27n without it. For 7 reaches without a budget that is about 1010 numbers, or 84 GB. The factored backup avoids this table, but the coupling matrix G\mathbf GG alone has 9n9^n9n entries: 43 million for 8 reaches, and about 3.5×1093.5\times10^93.5×109, or 28 GB, for 10. On the machine that built the figures, the 8-reach model took about 10 s to build and a few seconds to solve, and the 7-reach model without a budget took several times as long to solve as with it. Timings vary from run to run; the growth does not. The same blow-up hits the actions. The budget keeps the joint action set at 2n+12n+12n+1, but without it the minimization in each backup ranges over 3n3^n3n joint actions.

The model is a teaching version of the benchmark. The parameter values for mortality, seed output, dispersal, treatment success, costs and the discount factor come from Alkaee Taleghan et al. (2015), and the competitive advantage from Hall et al. (2012), but the river, the one-site reaches, the geometric dispersal kernel, the Poisson seed rain and the order of events within a year are our choices, and no field data enter the model. Real rivers have hundreds of reaches and many sites per reach. Alkaee Taleghan et al. (2015) describe the full dynamics as a dynamic Bayesian network too complex for exact inference, and plan from a simulator instead. The example still shows the point that the rest of the book builds on. Value iteration and policy iteration converge in a number of steps that hardly depends on the size of the river, but each step touches every state, and the number of states is exponential in the number of reaches. Managing a real river needs value functions that are represented compactly and backups that are estimated from samples, which is the subject of approximate Bellman equations and fitted Q-iteration.

Summary and Outlook¶

Discounting converts an infinite stream of rewards into a bounded value and makes the Bellman maps contractions in the sup norm. Value iteration applies successive approximation; policy iteration alternates a fixed-policy linear solve with greedy improvement. The inference-scheduling example also shows the price of state reduction: a smaller MDP averages over distinctions that can still affect future completions.

The hard maximum in the Bellman operator selects one action and is nondifferentiable at ties. Can the decision rule remain stochastic while the operator becomes smooth? Smooth and regularized dynamic programming answers by placing a convex regularizer on the action distribution.

Self-checks¶

Exercise 1 (Contraction factor)

If two value functions differ by at most ε\varepsilonε in sup norm, by at most how much can their discounted Bellman updates differ?

Solution to Exercise 1

At most γε\gamma\varepsilonγε. The discounted Bellman operator is a γ\gammaγ-contraction in the sup norm.

Exercise 2 (Residual certificate)

Value iteration produces a Bellman residual ∥Tv−v∥∞=0.02\|Tv-v\|_\infty=0.02∥Tv−v∥∞​=0.02 with γ=0.9\gamma=0.9γ=0.9. Give the standard upper bound on ∥v−v∗∥∞\|v-v^*\|_\infty∥v−v∗∥∞​.

Solution to Exercise 2

∥v−v∗∥∞≤∥Tv−v∥∞/(1−γ)=0.02/0.1=0.2\|v-v^*\|_\infty\leq \|Tv-v\|_\infty/(1-\gamma)=0.02/0.1=0.2∥v−v∗∥∞​≤∥Tv−v∥∞​/(1−γ)=0.02/0.1=0.2.

Exercise 3 (Evaluation versus improvement)

Which step of policy iteration requires solving a linear fixed-policy problem, and which step takes an actionwise maximum?

Solution to Exercise 3

Policy evaluation solves (I−γPπ)v=rπ(I-\gamma P_\pi)v=r_\pi(I−γPπ​)v=rπ​. Policy improvement computes action values from that vvv and chooses a greedy action in each state.

Exercise 4 (Reduced scheduling state)

Name one pair of request-level serving states that map to the same reduced state (p,d,a)(p,d,a)(p,d,a) but can have different future completion distributions.

Solution to Exercise 4

Two states can have the same numbers of waiting and decoding requests and the same oldest prefill-age bin while their active requests have different remaining output lengths. The reduced state discards those lengths, so its transition kernel averages over them.
